C337.definition: User categorization is a method that allows designers to gain a starting point for understanding users by classifying them into distinct groups based on their experience level.

C338.name: Usability
C338.definition: Usability is a measure of how good a system is from the perspective of the user. Usability encompasses the metrics used to determine how well a system performs for the user.

C339.name: User-centric design
C339.definition: User-centric design is a concept that can be viewed differently by various stakeholders, such as designers, depending on their specific role in the product development process.

C340.name: User interface designer
C340.definition: User interface designer is primarily concerned with the creative design of interface elements and layouts, which is informed by the characteristics of the user.

C341.name: Application software developer
C341.definition: Application software developer is primarily concerned with the development of software, which is the main focus when building a system.

C342.name: Development lifecycle
C342.definition: Development lifecycle is a structured process that must be followed when building software to ensure it accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations, making the system easier to use.

C343.name: Specified context of use
C343.definition: Specified context of use is the particular environment or scenario in which a product is designed to be used. Usability is ideally restricted to this specific context rather than all possible usage scenarios.

C344.name: Effectiveness
C344.definition: Effectiveness is one of the crucial criteria used to judge a product's usability. It relates to the ability of the user to achieve their specified goals when using the product.

C345.name: Efficiency
C345.definition: Efficiency refers to how quickly the user can perform the tasks they want to accomplish using the system. This measure focuses on the speed and resource usage of user interaction.

C346.name: Satisfaction
C346.definition: Satisfaction refers to the degree to which the user feels content while using the system. This measure assesses the user's overall positive or negative emotional state during interaction.

C347.name: Extended reality systems
C347.definition: Extended reality systems are the subject of discussion, focusing on creating a relationship between the user and the virtual environment. This relationship is built using both software and hardware components.

C348.name: Interaction design
C348.definition: Interaction design is the process of modeling how to provide input from the user's point of view, focusing on how easily the user can provide that input. This is a key part of the user-centered design approach.

C349.name: Perceptual design and modeling
C349.definition: Perceptual design and modeling is crucial for determining how well the output is generated, ensuring that the generated stimuli are appropriately perceived by the user. This is important because generating and perceiving stimuli are both vital for the system's effectiveness.

C350.name: XR engine
C350.definition: The XR engine is the middleware component within the system that utilizes hardware resources to generate output data. It processes the input data received from the user and system components.

C351.name: Perceptual design
C351.definition: Perceptual design is related to ensuring that the output generated for the user is appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived. It is one of the two critical design elements alongside interaction design.

C352.name: Perceptual system
C352.definition: Perceptual system is the mechanism that dictates how our senses and perception function, driven by underlying physiology. Understanding this system is necessary to understand how we experience interactive and extended reality systems.

C353.name: Immersion
C353.definition: Immersion is the feeling that a user is immersed in the virtual environment, which is achieved through interactions designed into the VR system. This feeling is essentially the perception that the user is immersed.

C354.name: Perceptual psychology
C354.definition: Perceptual psychology is the scientific study of how the brain transforms sensory input into experiences that are perceived. This science helps understand the relationship between external signals and the phenomena we consciously experience.

C355.name: Sensor
C355.definition: Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals within a circuit. This term is used when discussing a technological system or device.

C356.name: Human bodily sensor
C356.definition: Human bodily sensor is a body organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses. This term refers to the sensory organs found within the human body.

C357.name: Mechanoreceptor
C357.definition: A mechanoreceptor is a receptor that senses motion, vibration, or gravitational force. These receptors are involved in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.

C358.name: Chemoreceptor
C358.definition: A chemoreceptor is a receptor that provides signals based on the chemical composition of matter. These receptors are used for the senses of taste and smell.

C359.name: Vestibular organ
C359.definition: Vestibular organ is the sense organ that detects gravity or acceleration. It is specifically responsible for the sense of balance.

C360.name: Photoreceptor
C360.definition: A photoreceptor is a receptor found in the eyes. It targets electromagnetic energy, specifically in the frequency range of visible light.

C361.name: Receptor
C361.definition: A receptor is a sensor that is part of a sensory organ. It is designed to target particular stimuli.

C362.name: Sensory system selectivity
C362.definition: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon where a receptor is designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. This ensures the receptor targets particular stimuli.

C363.name: Perception
C363.definition: Perception is an abstract, higher-level activity that occurs after sense organs convert stimuli into neural impulses. This process is responsible for how we perceive things.

C364.name: Neuron
C364.definition: Neuron is a basic unit of the brain that contains a nucleus, dendrites, and an axon. These parts allow the neuron to receive and transmit impulses.

C365.name: Synapse
C365.definition: Synapse is a gap between the axon of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron. Communication occurs across this gap via electrical or chemical signals.

C366.name: Cerebral cortex
C366.definition: Cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that handles perception and other functions like attention, memory, and language. Roughly 20 billion neurons are devoted to this task.

C367.name: Sensory organ
C367.definition: Sensory organ is a biological component whose workings and implications are relevant for building Extended Reality (XR) systems. The lecture plans to cover these organs in detail in subsequent lectures.

C368.name: Hierarchical processing
C368.definition: Hierarchical processing is a type of neural processing that occurs in stages, where signals move from initial receptor inputs through successive levels of aggregation until they reach the cerebral cortex. This staged approach allows the detection of increasingly complex patterns within a stimulus.

C369.name: Selectivity
C369.definition: Selectivity is the characteristic of a receptor where it responds only to a narrow range of stimuli. This narrow range can be defined across various dimensions, including time, space, or frequency.

C370.name: Stimuli interpretation
C370.definition: Stimuli interpretation is the process where the meaning of a stimulus is determined, and it is not based solely on the sensory inputs received. It also depends heavily on the real-life experience and knowledge a person possesses.

C371.name: Perceptual phenomena
C371.definition: Perceptual phenomena are the results of combining sensory input with existing knowledge, and they include abilities such as face recognition or identifying a song.

C372.name: Perceptual processing
C372.definition: Perceptual processing is the overall outcome of combining real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience. This process is also described as hierarchical processing.

C373.name: Long-term memory
C373.definition: Long-term memory is where knowledge and life experience are stored, representing information that has been gained or learned over an extended period of time.

C374.name: Proprioception
C374.definition: Proprioception is a form of perception that allows the body to sense the relative positions of its parts and the muscular effort used during movement. This sense is unique because it does not rely on a dedicated sensory organ or receptor.

C375.name: Efference copies
C375.definition: Efference copies are signals sent by the motor cortex to other parts of the brain. These signals communicate the specific motions that have been executed by the body.

C376.name: Sixth sense
C376.definition: Sixth sense refers to a type of perception that functions without a dedicated sensory organ or receptor. This sense is derived from processing information sent by the motor cortex to understand body position and effort.

C377.name: Sensory conflict
C377.definition: Sensory conflict is a situation where different sensory inputs, such as vision and proprioception, report contradictory information to the brain.

C378.name: Brain development
C378.definition: Brain development is essentially the process of learning, which involves the brain learning the processes of perception and cognition over a long period of time.

C379.name: Human physiology
C379.definition: Human physiology is a basic concept studied in the context of designing Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It provides foundational knowledge about the body's functions relevant to XR design.

C380.name: Visual perception
C380.definition: Visual perception is the process where light arrives on the retina, which is part of the eye, leading to the perception of the scene. This process is guided by both engineered and natural lenses.

C381.name: Natural lens
C381.definition: Natural lens is the part of the eyes that is used in the combined lens system. Our eyes naturally contain lenses that contribute to visual perception.

C382.name: Light propagation
C382.definition: Light propagation is the movement of light through the combination of lenses. This process eventually leads to the perception of the scene.

C383.name: Retina
C383.definition: Retina is a component located at the back side of the eye where the light rays are focused to form images.

C384.name: Photon
C384.definition: A photon is a tiny particle of energy that moves through space at high speeds. These energy particles are often referred to as light particles.

C385.name: Wave
C385.definition: A wave is a ripple that travels through space. This description of light as a wave is helpful for understanding the spectrum of color.

C386.name: Ray
C386.definition: A ray is a trajectory or path assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon. This concept of light as a ray is helpful in explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

C387.name: Transmission
C387.definition: Transmission is the process where a part of a light ray passes through a material and exits the material. This allows the object to allow light to pass through it.

C388.name: Absorption
C388.definition: Absorption occurs when a portion of a light ray is absorbed within the material, causing the ray to terminate inside the object. There is no further propagation of the ray outside the material.

C389.name: Reflection
C389.definition: Reflection is the phenomenon where a light ray falls on a surface and bounces off without entering or penetrating the object. The ray gets reflected from the surface.

C390.name: Color perception
C390.definition: Color perception is the process where a viewer perceives a color based on the intensity of light that reaches their eye. This light is determined by how light rays interact with the surface of an object.

C391.name: Ambient light
C391.definition: Ambient light is the light present in the environment that reaches the eye. This light is reflected from the object surface and combines with light coming from a direct source.

C392.name: Cornea
C392.definition: Cornea is an outer surface component of the eye that refracts light rays as they pass through it.

C393.name: Pupil
C393.definition: Pupil is a component of the eye that is located between the cornea and the lens.

C394.name: Lens
C394.definition: Lens is a component of the eye that refracts light rays, working in sequence with the cornea to focus images.

C395.name: Iris
C395.definition: Iris is the structure that controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.

C396.name: Rods
C396.definition: Rods are photoreceptors found in the peripheral region of the retina, mixed with a lesser amount of cones. This region is particularly effective at detecting movement.

C397.name: Cones
C397.definition: Cones are a type of photoreceptor that are mainly located in a small central region of the retina, which is called the fovea.

C398.name: Fovea
C398.definition: Fovea is the central region of the retina that possesses the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, specifically cones. This region is responsible for contributing to the perception of central vision.

C399.name: Photopic vision
C399.definition: Photopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with cones, which allows for the perception of colors and is associated with central vision.

C400.name: Scotopic vision
C400.definition: Scotopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with rods, which is related to peripheral vision and allows weak lights to be visible as a series of grays.

C401.name: Image acuity
C401.definition: Image acuity is the ability to perceive fine detail, which is aided by having one optic nerve fiber for each cone.

C402.name: Visible light
C402.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves. This range encompasses the light waves that fall between the red and violet ends of the spectrum.

C403.name: Central vision
C403.definition: Central vision is one of the two types of vision supported by human eyes, which is enabled by the high concentration of cones found in the fovea. This type of vision allows the perception of a sharp color image when the eyes are pointed straight at a target.

C404.name: Peripheral vision
C404.definition: Peripheral vision is the other type of vision supported by human eyes, which relies on the peripheral region of the retina. This region has a lower density of photoreceptors and is better at detecting movement than central vision.

C405.name: Blind spot
C405.definition: Blind spot is a region in the eye where the individual cannot perceive light or visual stimuli. This area is blind because it lacks photoreceptors.

C406.name: Image surface
C406.definition: Image surface is the area of the eye where light rays fall, which is characterized as a non-planar surface. This surface is where the light is received before being transmitted to the brain.

C407.name: Engineered lens
C407.definition: Engineered lens is an artificially created lens used in setups to model optical concepts for comparison with biological systems. It is designed to converge parallel lights to a specific focal point.

C408.name: Focal plane
C408.definition: Focal plane is the specific plane where parallel lights converge when passing through an engineered lens. The distance between the lens and this focal point is known as the focal depth.

C409.name: Refractive index
C409.definition: Refractive index is a property of a medium that quantifies the amount of light that passes through it. This index is unique to each medium and affects how light travels through it.

C410.name: Focal point
C410.definition: Focal point is the specific point on the retina center where light rays are converged after passing through the eye's lenses. This point is where the image of the object is formed.

C411.name: Combined power
C411.definition: Combined power is the total optical strength achieved when multiple lenses, such as the cornea and the natural lens, are used together. This combined power determines whether faraway objects are focused correctly onto the retina.

C412.name: Diopter
C412.definition: Diopter is a unit of measurement used to quantify the optical power of a lens. This measurement is necessary to determine if the eye has sufficient power to focus light correctly.

C413.name: Convex lens
C413.definition: Convex lens is an optical component that increases optical power, functioning similarly to reading glasses. It is used inside the VR headset to help focus light onto the retina.

C414.name: Virtual image
C414.definition: Virtual image is the appearance of the screen as an enormous image that is perceived as being infinitely far away.

C415.name: Real image
C415.definition: Real image is an image that is nevertheless projected onto the retina. Perception of the world requires that real images are formed on the retina.

C416.name: Focal distance
C416.definition: Focal distance is the specific distance between the screen and the engineered lens that must be maintained for the best user experience. The engineered lens is usually placed at this distance.

C417.name: Binocular vision
C417.definition: Binocular vision is the process of looking at something using both eyes. It involves both eyes seeing the same image within a common region.

C418.name: Degrees of freedom
C418.definition: Degrees of freedom is a concept that indicates the different ways an object can move in space. There can be a total of six degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space.

C419.name: Translational movement
C419.definition: Translational movement is a type of movement used for navigating within a three-dimensional space. This movement is used for navigating in the 3D space.

C420.name: Rotational movement
C420.definition: Rotational movement is a type of movement primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis. Broadly, these two types of motions can be found in any virtual world.

C421.name: Yaw
C421.definition: Yaw is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom. Yaw is one of the specific rotational movements that can be observed.

C422.name: Roll
C422.definition: Roll is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom. Roll is one of the specific rotational movements that can be observed.

C423.name: Photoreceptor density
C423.definition: Photoreceptor density refers to basic physiological properties that directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware. This knowledge determines how display hardware is designed.

C424.name: Spatial resolution
C424.definition: Spatial resolution is a consideration that determines how many pixels are needed within a specific square area. This metric is crucial for designing effective displays.

C425.name: Intensity resolution and range
C425.definition: Intensity resolution and range define how many intensity values a display can produce, along with the minimum and maximum values. These values must be determined based on how many values can be processed without compromising perceptual quality.

C426.name: Temporal resolution
C426.definition: Temporal resolution is a consideration that dictates how fast displays need to change their pixels. This is also referred to as the refreshing or frame rate.

C427.name: VR displays
C427.definition: VR displays are engineered systems that should ideally be designed to perfectly match the performance of the visual sense they are trying to fool. This design goal requires understanding the limits of human perception.

C428.name: Aliasing
C428.definition: Aliasing is the visual effect where a sharp diagonal line appears jagged or stair-stepped when the image is zoomed out. This effect occurs when the display cannot accurately represent fine details.

C429.name: Screen door effect
C429.definition: Screen door effect is an image artifact commonly seen in LCD projectors that makes it appear as if there is a physical screen overlaying the image. This happens due to the way the image is displayed.

C430.name: Retina display
C430.definition: Retina display is a type of display that requires a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) to achieve a high level of visual clarity. This concept is suitable for displays viewed from a distance.

C431.name: Pixel density
C431.definition: Pixel density is the required measure of how many pixels a display needs to have. This density ensures that individual pixels or aliasing effects are not perceived by the viewer.

C432.name: Frame rates
C432.definition: Frame rates measure the number of images displayed per second, and for immersive environments, they must be significantly higher than those typically seen on standard desktop or television displays.

C433.name: Physiology of human vision
C433.definition: Physiology of human vision refers to the biological makeup of our eyes. This knowledge helps explain how we perceive various elements such as color, depth, and scenes.

C434.name: XR systems
C434.definition: XR systems are the technological frameworks that utilize principles of visual perception. These systems are designed to create Extended Reality experiences, and they require careful management of factors like resolutions and frame rates.

C435.name: Auditory sense
C435.definition: Auditory sense is the human ability to perceive sound, and the lecture will cover its physiology and relevance to extended reality experiences. This sense is the primary focus of the current lecture.

C436.name: Sound
C436.definition: Sound is defined as a wave. This wave is the physical phenomenon that is converted into neural impulses by the ear.

C437.name: Frequency
C437.definition: Frequency is the number of alterations between one maximum to another maximum per second, which is measured in Hertz.

C438.name: Outer ear
C438.definition: The outer ear is the initial part of the human hearing system that receives sound waves. It contains components like the canal, which amplifies sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

C439.name: Middle ear
C439.definition: The middle ear is the section of the hearing system located after the outer ear. It houses the three bones, known as ossicles, which transfer vibrations.

C440.name: Inner ear
C440.definition: The inner ear is the final part of the human hearing system, which is roughly the size of a marble. It contains the cochlea, the organ responsible for hearing.

C441.name: Tympanic membrane
C441.definition: The tympanic membrane is a structure in the middle ear that vibrates when a sound wave passes through the outer ear canal. This vibration initiates the transfer of sound energy.

C442.name: Cochlea
C442.definition: The cochlea is the sense organ housed within the inner ear. It converts incoming sound energy, which is a wave, into neural impulses for transmission to the brain.

C443.name: Auditory system
C443.definition: Auditory system is the mechanism that excites the hearing system. It converts sound waves into neural impulses which are then transmitted to the brain for perception.

C444.name: Auditory perception
C444.definition: Auditory perception is the process of understanding how we perceive sound, which is crucial for creating immersive experiences in extended reality systems.

C445.name: Social level
C445.definition: Social level perception is the type of perception that helps individuals carry out social interactions with others.

C446.name: Warning level
C446.definition: Warning level perception provides an alert or warning about a specific event or situation.

C447.name: Primitive level
C447.definition: Primitive level perception is generally the intuitive understanding of sound, often relating to background noises that individuals tend to ignore.

C448.name: Psychophysics
C448.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that result from physical stimuli. It is defined as a broader field of study.

C449.name: Psychoacoustics
C449.definition: Psychoacoustics is a specific area of psychophysics that focuses on sound. It is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli.

C450.name: Stevens' power law
C450.definition: Stevens' power law is a well-known result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude. This relationship is mathematically represented as P equals Cm to the power x.

C451.name: Just noticeable difference
C451.definition: Just noticeable difference (JND) is a well-known result from psychophysics that refers to the minimum amount a stimulus must change for subjects to perceive the change in at least 50% of trials.

C452.name: Weber's law
C452.definition: Weber's law is a law used to capture the Just noticeable difference (JND). It is represented by the formula delta M by M equals C, where C is a constant.

C453.name: Loudness perception
C453.definition: Loudness perception is the ability to perceive the volume of a sound, which can be analyzed using established psychophysical or psychoacoustic theories. These theories are used to design effective auditory systems.

C454.name: Pitch perception
C454.definition: Pitch perception is one of the specific levels of sound perception that must be accounted for when generating sound in an embedded system. It is a factor that contributes to the overall quality of the immersive experience.

C455.name: Localization
C455.definition: Localization is a kind of perception that involves determining the source of a sound. This perception is a key element that must be implemented for the best immersive experience.

C456.name: Azimuth
C456.definition: Azimuth is the angle measured in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the sound source. This angle represents the vector projected onto the horizontal plane.

C457.name: Elevation
C457.definition: Elevation is the angle that corresponds to the deviation of the sound source from the horizontal plane. This angle is measured between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane.

C458.name: Interaural Level Difference
C458.definition: Interaural Level Difference (ILD) is the difference in sound magnitude as perceived by each ear. This difference can occur when one ear is facing the sound source while the other is in an acoustic shadow.

C459.name: Interaural Time Difference
C459.definition: Interaural Time Difference (ITD) is the difference in the arrival time of a sound source to each ear. This difference is caused by the physical distance between the two ears.

C460.name: Head-related transfer function
C460.definition: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) are necessary to implement localization in sound systems. Generally, these functions are implemented for the average human user, although individual variations exist.

C461.name: Binaural sound
C461.definition: Binaural sound is synthesized using a pair of Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTF) for both ears. This synthesis allows for the accurate implementation of localization effects.

C462.name: Full immersive experience
C462.definition: Full immersive experience is the topic of discussion that involves the role of senses beyond the visual and auditory senses.

C463.name: Human visual perceptual system
C463.definition: Human visual perceptual system is the system whose knowledge assists in the construction of better Extended Reality (XR) systems. This system is one of the senses discussed in detail.

C464.name: Human auditory system
C464.definition: Human auditory system is a sensory system that helps create an immersive experience within Extended Reality (XR). It works in addition to the visual perceptual system.

C465.name: Kinesthesis
C465.definition: Kinesthesis provides information regarding velocities, acceleration, and forces while moving body parts. It is the awareness of various parameters associated with movement.

C466.name: Haptic perception
C466.definition: Haptic perception is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects. This shape is inferred through the process of haptic exploration, which involves object handling.

C467.name: Muscle spindle
C467.definition: Muscle spindle is a receptor embedded inside each muscle. It reports to the brain about changes in the length of the muscle whenever movement occurs.

C468.name: Golgi tendon organ
C468.definition: Golgi tendon organ is a receptor embedded in tendons, which are tough bands connecting muscles to bones. It reports changes in muscle tension associated with muscle movement.

C469.name: Haptic exploration
C469.definition: Haptic explorations are methods of perceiving the world through touch. These explorations allow us to perceive the geometric properties of objects around us.

C470.name: Force feedback
C470.definition: Force feedback is a method of providing touch sensation stimuli, typically delivered through vibrations from XR applications. Force feedback devices are commonly used in VR systems, such as smart gloves or body suits, to allow users to experience physical forces.

C471.name: Haptic pin array
C471.definition: Haptic pin array is a device containing a matrix of pins that is controlled by a computer system. The pins are forced upward as the user's fingertip scans the surface, simulating various textures of an object.

C472.name: Tangible user interface
C472.definition: Tangible user interface is a method where real-world objects are used to provide feedback to the somatosensory system. This approach replaces computer-controlled haptic devices by allowing users to interact with physical objects whose virtual avatars exist in the world.

C473.name: Smell interface
C473.definition: Smell interface is a device intended to provide chemical stimuli to the nose. It typically utilizes air pumps to spray chemical compounds into the air.

C474.name: Olfactory display
C474.definition: Olfactory display is a generic term used to refer to systems that function as smell interfaces. These displays are designed to generate and deliver odor stimuli to the user.

C475.name: Taste interface
C475.definition: Taste interface is a device used to simulate the sensation of taste electronically. This simulation often requires placing electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation.

C476.name: Human somatosensory system
C476.definition: Human somatosensory system is the biological mechanism related to the perception of touch and proprioception. This system utilizes several receptors dedicated to sensing different aspects of the body and environment.

C477.name: Immersion
C477.definition: Immersion is a quality that can be increased when support is provided in a Virtual Reality or Extended Reality setting. This support helps the user feel more deeply involved in the virtual environment.

C478.name: Interactive system
C478.definition: Interactive system is a type of software system that requires an empirical study stage to ensure it conforms to usability. This requirement differentiates it from other software systems.

C479.name: Usability
C479.definition: Usability is the quality metric that ensures a product conforms to the needs and expectations of the end user. Usability is what is assessed during empirical studies.

C480.name: Software development life cycle
C480.definition: Software development life cycle is a process followed to develop and deploy software. This cycle comprehensively captures and represents the design and development activities required for building the software.

C481.name: Software engineering
C481.definition: Software engineering is the single term used to represent the idea of software development life cycle. It involves the structured process of engineering a software.

C482.name: Stages
C482.definition: Stages are the components that capture or structure the whole development process. Through their connection, they represent how the development process should take place to achieve the desired outcome.

C483.name: Usable software
C483.definition: Usable software is the desired output of the development process. It is the functional software application that the systematic process aims to produce.

C484.name: Design space
C484.definition: Design space is the set of all possible designs for a given problem. The size of this space is determined by the number of elements that must be placed on a screen.

C485.name: Highly iterative lifecycle
C485.definition: A highly iterative lifecycle is a software development lifecycle that requires frequent looping between stages. This structure is necessary to account for user feedback and implement a user-centric design approach.

C486.name: Design prototype evaluate cycle
C486.definition: The Design prototype evaluate cycle is a specific phase within the development process. This cycle comprises the design stage, prototyping stage, and early evaluation stage.

C487.name: Requirement gathering stage
C487.definition: Requirement gathering stage is the initial phase where the project's needs are identified, focusing specifically on gathering requirements from end users in addition to the client. This stage involves methods like contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes to understand user needs

C488.name: Design prototype evaluate loop
C488.definition: Design prototype evaluate loop is an iterative process required for refining early designs based on feedback provided by users. This loop involves creating a prototype, evaluating it, identifying problems, and then modifying the design repeatedly until significant problems cease to be identified

C489.name: Interface design
C489.definition: Interface design is one of the two activities included in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle. Interface design focuses on the visual and functional aspects of the system from the user's point of view

C490.name: Code design
C490.definition: Code design is a highly skilled and costly process that requires skilled manpower and is the initial stage of the development life cycle. Code design is often revisited if issues are found during testing.

C491.name: Empirical study
C491.definition: Empirical study is a unique stage in interactive system development that involves systematic testing with end users. This stage is required to ensure the product conforms to usability.

C492.name: Interactive System Development Lifecycle
aliases: Interactive system development life cycles (Agile development idea)
C492.definition: Interactive System Development Lifecycle is the overall idea or process used to build interactive systems.

C493.name: Digital preservation
C493.definition: Digital preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources. This method allows for the preservation of information in a digital form.

C494.name: Satra
C494.definition: Satra is an authoritative center of Vaishnavite faith in Assam that functions as a living workshop for various visual and performing arts.

C495.name: Tangible heritage
C495.definition: Tangible heritage refers to heritage aspects of the island that are physical and can be touched or felt, such as cultural artifacts or architectural structures.

C496.name: Intangible heritage
C496.definition: Intangible heritage consists of aspects that cannot be physically touched or felt but are sensed through various means, including traditional skills, knowledge, and performing arts.

C497.name: Cultural heritage
C497.definition: Cultural heritage is a broad aspect encompassing both tangible and intangible heritage that forms part of the island's cultural identity.

C498.name: Ecological heritage
C498.definition: Ecological heritage refers to the flora and fauna of an island that exists due to its unique geology, geography, and topography. This heritage is a key resource that must be preserved.

C499.name: Erosion
C499.definition: Erosion is the process where the island is constantly hit by severe annual floods, causing the land and habitable areas to disappear. This process endangers both the rich cultural resources and the material existence of the island itself.

C500.name: Archiving
C500.definition: Archiving means storing the visual and audio files that capture the heritage information of a particular entity, object, space, or place. This process is a key component of digital preservation.

C501.name: Digital avatar
C501.definition: Digital avatar is a digital representation created in the digital space of elements and objects from a physical space. This allows for the preservation of fragile artifacts that might not survive over time.

C502.name: Heritage preservation
C502.definition: Heritage preservation is the process of creating an archive of heritage information, which ideally consists of multimedia such as images, videos, audios, and texts. This archive utilizes different sorts of media to document the heritage.

C503.name: User experience
C503.definition: User experience is a major issue concerning the quality of the user's interaction with the virtual environment. This aspect determines how effectively users engage with the system.

C504.name: Immersive VR experience
C504.definition: Immersive VR experience is a proposed method to expose users to the heritage aspects of Majuli. This type of experience aims to provide a highly engaging and realistic virtual environment.

C505.name: Immersive virtual tours
C505.definition: Immersive virtual tours are a component of the digital heritage preservation system that allows users to experience the heritage virtually. These tours enable users to explore the island in a simulated environment.

C506.name: Hot spot
C506.definition: Hot spot is a specific location identified on a map of the island where the tangible and intangible aspects are captured. Capturing these spots allows for the comprehensive capture of the island's entire cultural landscape.

C507.name: Multimodal archive
C507.definition: Multimodal archive is a collection created to preserve heritage aspects by combining various data types. This archive includes images, 3D models, videos, and textual descriptions of artifacts.

C508.name: Usability testing
C508.definition: Usability testing is a method of evaluation that focuses primarily on how easy a design is to use. This testing is the main focus, rather than solely checking the underlying code.

C509.name: Tangible and intangible heritage
C509.definition: Tangible and intangible heritage refers to the vast information captured about the island. This information includes both physical artifacts and non-physical cultural elements.

C510.name: Requirement gathering
C510.definition: Requirement gathering is the process of learning about end-user needs and is a key stage in system development. This process aims to gather end-user requirements so that the resulting design ensures usability.

C511.name: Specification
C511.definition: Specification is the formal documentation required for system implementation. It details the requirements that have been gathered from the end users.

C512.name: Usability
C512.definition: Usability is a quality that is measured against a specified context of use. Ensuring usability requires knowing how users behave within that specific work context.

C513.name: System-centered design
C513.definition: System-centered design is an approach where the development is driven by the skill and interest of the developer or manager. The main concerns of this design focus on what the developer can easily build using available tools.

C514.name: End user requirement
C514.definition: End user requirements are the needs and goals of the people who will use the system. Gathering these requirements requires first knowing and specifying who those users are.

C515.name: Feasibility
C515.definition: Feasibility refers to requirements related to the practical aspects of development. These requirements include decisions such as developing for a mobile platform or selecting a programming language.

C516.name: Usability requirements
C516.definition: Usability requirements are end user requirements gathered through methods like contextual inquiry. These requirements define the quality of a product when measured against a specified context of use.

C517.name: Non-functional requirements
C517.definition: Non-functional requirements are system characteristics that cannot be expressed as functions. These requirements are generally treated as a type of requirement.

C518.name: Functional requirements
C518.definition: Functional requirements refer to system features and abilities of the system to carry out tasks. These functions are treated as black boxes, generating an output from a provided input.

C519.name: Quality attributes
C519.definition: Quality attributes are characteristics of the software that usability requirements are typically related to.

C520.name: Interface issues
C520.definition: Interface issues refers to the design or the qualities of an interface that must be usable. These issues cover how the system interfaces with its environment, users, and other systems.

C521.name: Requirement gathering methods
C521.definition: Requirement gathering methods are the techniques that can be deployed to collect requirements and ensure usability.

C522.name: External system interface
C522.definition: External system interface refers to the interfacing between hardware and software, as well as the user interface. This interface is where usability issues come into the picture.

C523.name: Contextual inquiry
C523.definition: Contextual inquiry is an end user requirement gathering method used to collect requirements. This method involves observing users while they perform tasks within their natural work setting.

C524.name: Natural work setting
C524.definition: Natural work setting is the specific environment where users perform tasks. This setting serves as the specified context of use for gathering end user requirements.

C525.name: Semi-structured interview process
C525.definition: Semi-structured interview process is a method of contextual inquiry that combines two elements. These elements are both interviews and observations of the user.

C526.name: Usability requirement gathering
C526.definition: Usability requirement gathering is an essential process for ensuring a usable design, which involves collecting the needs and expectations of users. This process ensures that the final design properly addresses the users' needs.

C527.name: Contextual inquiry
C527.definition: Contextual inquiry is a systematic process used to carry out an inquiry by observing users in their natural environment. This process is broken down into five distinct stages.

C528.name: Passive mode
C528.definition: Passive mode involves recording or videotaping user activities without an observer present during the activity. The recorded activities are then observed later by the researcher.

C529.name: Master apprentice model
C529.definition: The master apprentice model is a principle during inquiry where the observer acts as the apprentice and treats the users as the masters. The purpose of this model is to learn user behavior rather than instructing users.

C530.name: Plan stage
C530.definition: The plan stage involves planning the activities of the inquiry, which includes identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, and arranging methods for recording observations.

C531.name: Initiate stage
C531.definition: The initiate stage requires contacting relevant authorities to obtain necessary permissions and establishing open communication with end users to reduce their anxieties about the observation.

C532.name: Reflect
C532.definition: Reflect is the final stage of the inquiry process, which involves analyzing the data that was gathered during the observation period.

C533.name: Execute stage
C533.definition: The execute stage is the phase where the actual inquiry takes place, meaning the observation of the users in their work setting occurs.

C534.name: Execute test stage
C534.definition: The execute test stage is the phase where observations are actually performed and data is recorded. This stage involves the practical execution of the testing process.

C535.name: Reflect stage
C535.definition: The reflect stage is the phase where the observer or experimental team analyzes the data that was collected. This analysis is performed to identify the necessary design goals.

C536.name: Affinity diagram method
C536.definition: Affinity diagram is the framework used when following the process of grouping notes. It is the structure that guides the organization of the collected data.

C537.name: Physical note-taking
C537.definition: Physical note-taking is the traditional method of recording information using pen and paper. This method serves as a baseline for comparison when developing digital note-taking applications.

C538.name: Idea generation
C538.definition: Idea generation refers to the final note that is taken by the observer. This process involves generating notes and subsequently refining them using better language.

C539.name: Groups
C539.definition: Groups are collections formed by identifying patterns among ideas so that similar ideas with similar patterns can be sorted together into a single unit.

C540.name: Header
C540.definition: Header is a pattern that is assigned to a group of ideas. This pattern defines the members of the group and binds the ideas together.

C541.name: Idea
C541.definition: Idea is a note taken by an observer that is used when following the affinity diagram. Ideas are the fundamental units that are generated during the observation process.

C542.name: Display
C542.definition: Display is the physical location, such as a wall or a board, where the collected ideas are put together. It serves as the central place for the generated notes.

C543.name: Requirement
C543.definition: Requirement is the identification of what needs to be done to make a product usable. It focuses on what must be achieved rather than how it must be implemented.

C544.name: Design recommendation
C544.definition: Design recommendation is a set of suggestions that can be developed based on the analysis of collected data. These recommendations serve as guidelines for the design process.

C545.name: Guidelines
C545.definition: Guidelines are initial design recommendations that can be derived from data collection but are not the complete requirements for implementation. These recommendations help guide the design process.

C546.name: Requirement gathering
C546.definition: Requirement gathering is the basic idea of collecting and understanding the needs and expectations of users for a system. This process determines what the final system must be able to do.

C547.name: Contextual inquiry
C547.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method used to obtain guidelines or requirements by observing users in their natural environment. This process helps identify usability requirements for a system.

C548.name: Usability
C548.definition: Usability is a prime concern in system development, and the objective is to ensure that the end product is usable. This concept is central to user-centered design.

C549.name: Software requirements specification (SRS) document
C549.definition: Software requirements specification (SRS) document is a formal document used to specify all types of requirements for a software project, including both functional and non-functional requirements.

C550.name: Functional requirement specification
C550.definition: Functional requirement specification is the formal representation or specification of requirements, detailing how a system must function.

C551.name: Hierarchical structure of requirements
C551.definition: Hierarchical structure of requirements is a convention used in specification where requirements are organized in levels, such as R1, R1.1, and so on, to represent functions.

C552.name: Design guideline
C552.definition: Design guideline is a set of rules or recommendations that can be converted from the output of contextual inquiry. These guidelines are used to ensure the usability of the subsequent design stages.

C553.name: Function
C553.definition: Function is a specific capability or unit of work within the system that performs a defined task. This function takes an input and generates a specific output.

C554.name: Functional specification
C554.definition: Functional specification is a type of specification used to document requirements. It is one of the methods discussed for specifying requirements.

C555.name: Know the user
C555.definition: Know the user is the first stage of the requirement gathering process. This stage involves identifying and understanding the different groups of people who will use the system.

C556.name: Subset of data
C556.definition: A subset of data is a limited portion of a larger data set that is made accessible to a specific user group. This approach reduces the overall expanse of information, which helps prevent user confusion and cyber sickness.

C557.name: Usable system
C557.definition: A usable system is a technology designed to be effective and functional for specific groups of users within a defined context. The usability of the system is targeted only for the identified user groups, not for all possible users.

C558.name: Location awareness
C558.definition: Location awareness is the ability to ensure users have accurate location information within a virtual environment. Location awareness prevents disorientation, which is especially crucial when users are exploring large geographical spaces.

C559.name: Tangible and intangible heritage experience
C559.definition: Tangible and intangible heritage experience refers to the need to provide users with both physical and non-physical cultural heritage. The challenge involves finding ways to combine these two types of heritage into a seamless experience.

C560.name: Interaction aid
C560.definition: Interaction aid is support provided to improve the overall user experience in a virtual environment. This support includes navigation assistance, user-friendly interfaces, and methods to increase presence through natural interactions.

C561.name: Contextual inquiry phase
C561.definition: Contextual inquiry phase is a stage of research used to identify specific issues faced by users. This phase helps pinpoint problems, such as location awareness issues, tailored to specific user groups.

C562.name: Design of immersive experiences
C562.definition: Design of immersive experiences is the process of planning and structuring the overall experience within virtual or augmented reality environments. This design focuses on creating a cohesive and engaging experience for the user.

C563.name: Interface and interaction design
C563.definition: Interface and interaction design is the design process that focuses on how a user interacts with a system, specifically addressing the interface and the overall interaction experience.

C564.name: Design language
C564.definition: Design language is the necessary framework used to express a design, allowing designers to brainstorm or refine the concepts they are developing.

C565.name: Heuristics
C565.definition: Heuristics are guidelines, thumb rules, or checklists that can be used as a starting point to aid the creative thinking process in design.

C566.name: Specification of design
C566.definition: Specification of design refers to the detailed description of how a system will be built. This concept is distinct from the specification of requirements.

C567.name: Prototype
C567.definition: Prototype is a tangible model that can be considered a language used to express design ideas. It serves as a language for interface design.

C568.name: Specific guideline
C568.definition: Specific guideline is a guideline that is applicable to particular systems or aspects, such as those designed to minimize cyber sickness in VR systems. These guidelines are typically relevant when immersion is a very important issue.

C569.name: Generic guideline
C569.definition: Generic guideline is a guideline that is applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality systems. These guidelines may not be fully applicable, but they are mostly applicable to extended reality systems.

C570.name: Internal consistency
C570.definition: Internal consistency means that the same elements and interactions should be utilized in other parts of the design when performing the same task. Separate objects or interactions should not be used for the same task in different usage instances.

C571.name: External consistency
C571.definition: External consistency ensures that the knowledge a user brings from the real world is as closely matching with their experience in the virtual world as possible. The elements and interactions performed should be close to real-world experience.

C572.name: Universal usability
C572.definition: Universal usability is a design principle that requires systems to be functional and accessible for all types of users. This approach ensures that the system supports diverse user needs rather than focusing on a single group.

C573.name: Informative feedback
C573.definition: Informative feedback is the provision of information to the user regarding the system's status or the outcome of their actions. This feedback helps the user understand what the system is doing and how much of a task has been completed.

C574.name: Usable design
C574.definition: Usable design is a quality of design where the user is able to understand the system's operations and the progress of a task. Lack of informative feedback makes a design unusable because the user cannot determine if the task is progressing or completed.

C575.name: Storage metaphor
C575.definition: Storage metaphor is a conceptual representation used in the interface to symbolize the function of storage. For instance, a floppy disk icon is used as a metaphor to represent the act of saving data.

C576.name: Closure
C576.definition: Closure is the feeling the user receives when they successfully complete an objective or task within the system. The system must be designed to indicate that the task has been started, executed, and finally completed.

C577.name: Activity grouping
C577.definition: Activity grouping is the design principle of organizing a task into distinct parts: a beginning, a middle, and an end. This structure helps the user understand the process and how to proceed toward achieving their goal.

C578.name: Error prevention
C578.definition: Error prevention is a design strategy that aims to minimize the possibility of users making mistakes in the first place. This is achieved by designing the system to keep error rates low.

C579.name: Reversal of action
C579.definition: Reversal of action is a design objective that allows users to undo or rectify mistakes by returning from an erroneous situation. This is often facilitated by facilities such as undo and redo.

C580.name: User control
C580.definition: User control is the design principle that ensures users feel they are in charge of the system. This feeling is crucial because users, especially lay persons, may lack technical expertise.

C581.name: Feedback
C581.definition: Feedback is the necessary visual confirmation that the user's actions are being processed. It ensures the user can perceive that a change in system state has occurred.

C582.name: Short term memory
C582.definition: Short term memory is a form of non-permanent storage that functions like a notebook, holding information brought from long-term memory to assist with daily activities.

C583.name: Long term memory
C583.definition: Long term memory is the permanent storage that holds information which is retrieved and brought into short-term memory to support current activities.

C584.name: Short term memory load
C584.definition: Short term memory load refers to the total amount of information that a user must actively hold in their short-term memory while operating an interface.

C585.name: Object interaction
C585.definition: Object interaction is the selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment. This process allows users to engage with elements within the virtual space.

C586.name: Navigation
C586.definition: Navigation refers to the act of moving from one specific point to another within the virtual environment. This allows the user to traverse the virtual space.

C587.name: Interaction for system control
C587.definition: Interaction for system control involves several system-related settings interactions. These interactions are required to change various settings within the system.

C588.name: Navigation
C588.definition: Navigation is the act of moving from one point to another within the virtual world, which requires a corresponding change in the user's viewpoint. This technique primarily involves movement rather than object engagement.

C589.name: Interaction for selection
C589.definition: Interaction for selection is the process of choosing a specific object from a set of objects within a virtual world. This action identifies the object that the user intends to interact with next.

C590.name: Interaction for manipulation
C590.definition: Interaction for manipulation is the subsequent action taken after an object has been selected. This interaction changes the properties of the object, such as its appearance or state.

C591.name: Object selection techniques
C591.definition: Object selection techniques refer to the methods used to specify one or more objects from a collection of virtual objects in a virtual world. These techniques determine how the user identifies the desired object.

C592.name: Target occlusion
C592.definition: Target occlusion occurs when a target object is partially or fully hidden by other surrounding objects in the virtual environment. This condition makes locating and selecting the target a challenging task for the user.

C593.name: Pointing-based selection
C593.definition: Pointing-based selection is a method of selecting objects in a virtual world that relies on pointing actions. This technique is one of several methods available for object selection.

C594.name: Image plane selection
C594.definition: Image plane selection is a method of selection where the user uses fingers or hands to pinpoint an object on a 2D view plane. This technique defines the object within the plane as viewed by the user from a distance.

C595.name: Hand selection technique
C595.definition: Hand selection technique is the method of selecting virtual objects within the virtual world using the user's hand. This category encompasses various techniques that utilize the hand for object interaction.

C596.name: Virtual hand
C596.definition: Virtual hand is an avatar of the physical hand that is visible in the virtual world. This virtual hand is tied to the user's physical hand, allowing for a direct one-to-one mapping of motion.

C597.name: Go-go technique
C597.definition: Go-go technique is a method designed to select distant objects without causing user fatigue. This technique allows the user to interactively change the length of the virtual arm.

C598.name: Prism
C598.definition: Prism is an improvement upon the go-go technique that controls movement based on speed. This technique applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's hand movement is slower than a specified minimum velocity.

C599.name: Intent-driven selection
C599.definition: Intent-driven selection is a method where the user indicates their desire to select an object using gestures or the posture of their virtual fingers. This technique allows the user to signal their confidence in selecting an object.

C600.name: Ray casting
C600.definition: Ray casting is a basic technique where the user points at objects using a virtual ray, which can be either a short line segment or an infinite line. This virtual ray is attached to the user's hand, head, or eye depending on the input device used.

C601.name: Bend cast
C601.definition: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting where the system bends the ray toward the object that is closest to the ray's path. This technique reduces the need for precise pointing by identifying the closest object.

C602.name: Depth ray
C602.definition: Depth ray is a technique used to resolve ambiguity when a pointing vector intersects multiple targets. It selects the object that is closest to a specific depth marker used for disambiguation.

C603.name: Eye gaze pointing
C603.definition: Eye gaze pointing is a method of pointing where the ray is extended and controlled by tracking the user's eye gaze using eye trackers. Changes in the user's eye gaze directly change the pointing direction.

C604.name: Volumetric selection
C604.definition: Volumetric selection enables the user to select a three-dimensional region within virtual space. Corresponding objects located within that defined 3D region are then selected.

C605.name: Head crusher technique
C605.definition: Head crusher technique involves the user positioning the thumb and forefinger around a desired object. The object is enclosed by the thumb and forefinger within the 2D image plane.

C606.name: Cone casting flashlight technique
C606.definition: Cone casting flashlight technique extends the ray casting idea by using a cone instead of a ray. A cone is cast to a distance, and all objects found within the cone's extent are selected.

C607.name: Two-handed box selection technique
C607.definition: Two-handed box selection technique allows the user to use both hands to define, orient, and shape a selection volume. This volume can be a cube, a box, or a rectangular parallelepiped.

C608.name: Manipulation
C608.definition: Manipulation is the process of modifying the properties of a selected object, such as its position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior. These properties are what are changed when using manipulation techniques.

C609.name: Hand manipulation
C609.definition: Hand manipulation uses a virtual hand, which can be implemented through smart gloves or gesture-based manipulation, to directly interact with and modify virtual objects. This method is considered the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

C610.name: Indirect manipulation
C610.definition: Indirect manipulation allows a user to modify a desired virtual object by interacting with a separate object that is mapped to it. This enables users to manipulate virtual objects without directly interacting with the virtual object itself.

C611.name: World in miniature
C611.definition: World in miniature is an indirect proxy technique that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment. The user can then indirectly manipulate the actual virtual object by interacting with its representation in this miniature model.

C612.name: Integrated hybrid manipulation
C612.definition: Integrated hybrid manipulation is a technique where the system automatically switches between selection and manipulation modes without explicit user input. It also switches back to selection mode after the manipulation task is finished.

C613.name: Navigation
C613.definition: Navigation is the process of moving the user from one point to another within the virtual world. This movement is characterized by a change in the user's field of view or viewpoint.

C614.name: Exploration
C614.definition: Exploration is a type of travel that occurs when there is no explicit goal for the user to reach. The user simply moves around to observe, learn, or explore the environment.

C615.name: Search
C615.definition: Search is a type of travel that involves moving toward or looking for a specified target location. This contrasts with exploration, as the user has a specific destination in mind.

C616.name: Maneuvering
C616.definition: Maneuvering refers to short, precise movements that change the point of view or viewpoint. This technique involves breaking down a larger path into smaller, focused segments.

C617.name: Wayfinding
C617.definition: Wayfinding is the necessary support required for a system to provide a good immersive user experience. Wayfinding support ensures that travel supports are effectively used and deployed by the user while they are navigating.

C618.name: Walking-based locomotion
C618.definition: Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual world by physically walking in the real world. It involves some form of physical movement that corresponds to virtual movement in the immersive environment.

C619.name: Partial gait technique
C619.definition: Partial gait technique refers to a scenario where the user walks but remains in the same physical location. The pattern of walking in that single place is mapped to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C620.name: Gait negation technique
C620.definition: Gait negation technique requires a specialized setup where the user's lateral movements are canceled, keeping their physical position fixed. The system then maps the remaining movement pattern to a specific type of virtual movement.

C621.name: Steering-based navigation
C621.definition: Steering-based navigation is a method that indicates continuous control of direction and speed while the user is moving from one point to another. Essentially, if a system implements continuous control over direction and speed, it utilizes this type of navigation.

C622.name: Spatial steering-based navigation
C622.definition: Spatial steering-based navigation is a type of steering-based navigation where the control is managed using the user's body parts or through physical steering-based hardware. This technique allows the user to control locomotion using either their body or specialized equipment.

C623.name: Selection-based navigation or locomotion technique
C623.definition: Selection-based navigation or locomotion technique allows users to focus on the destination rather than specifying how to reach it. Unlike previous techniques, the user selects where to go instead of continuously specifying the movement path.

C624.name: Target selection-based locomotion
C624.definition: Target selection-based locomotion occurs when the user selects a specific destination or target location. Upon selection, the virtual viewpoint changes, allowing the user to feel as if they have moved to the target.

C625.name: Manipulation-based locomotion techniques
C625.definition: Manipulation-based locomotion techniques work by manipulating the user's position, orientation, or scale. This manipulation is achieved using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

C626.name: Mental model
C626.definition: Mental model refers to the cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment that a user builds. This model allows the user to easily locate themselves and identify a suitable path to their destination.

C627.name: Landmark knowledge
C627.definition: Landmark knowledge is a type of spatial knowledge that refers to having knowledge about specific landmarks within the surroundings or in other locations. This knowledge is essential for constituting the overall mental model.

C628.name: Procedural knowledge
C628.definition: Procedural knowledge is a type of spatial knowledge that refers to the sequence of actions required to successfully follow a path. This knowledge is necessary for building the complete mental model of the environment.

C629.name: Topological knowledge
C629.definition: Topological knowledge is a type of spatial knowledge that refers to the overall map of the environment. This knowledge, along with landmark and procedural knowledge, forms the essential knowledge base for the mental model.

C630.name: Landmark
C630.definition: Landmark is any obvious, distinct, non-mobile object that is positioned within a given place. A good landmark must be clearly visible from different points of view and locations.

C631.name: Path following
C631.definition: Path following is a wayfinding support technique where multiple paths through a single space are denoted, often using colors. This allows the user to understand that various routes are available to reach a destination.

C632.name: Breadcrumbs
C632.definition: Breadcrumbs is a support idea that involves leaving a trail of markers along a path followed by predecessors. This trail allows users to know which paths have been explored, preventing them from getting lost.

C633.name: Navigation interaction
C633.definition: Navigation interaction is a technique that comprises the processes of travel and wayfinding within an environment. This interaction allows users to move through and locate themselves within a space.

C634.name: Multimodal interaction techniques
C634.definition: Multimodal interaction techniques are methods that combine multiple interaction techniques simultaneously for system control. For example, a user can combine voice commands with gestures to perform a task.

C635.name: Interface and interaction
C635.definition: Interface and interaction is the core idea of design that focuses on how a user engages with a system. This concept is fundamental to creating effective and usable software experiences.

C636.name: Interaction techniques
C636.definition: Interaction techniques are various methods typically used in immersive settings. These techniques include object interaction, navigation interaction, and interactions for system control.

C637.name: User presence
C637.definition: User presence is the goal of ensuring that users feel immersed and present within the virtual environment. This concept relates to the user's feeling of being physically located in the virtual space.

C638.name: User experience design
C638.definition: User experience design is the process of designing an experience by first identifying the user. This identification is the first stage in the overall experience design process.

C639.name: Contextual inquiry methods
C639.definition: Contextual inquiry methods are the techniques used to collect specific preferences from users. These methods help tailor the content and features of a virtual tour.

C640.name: Immersive setting
C640.definition: An immersive setting is a design element, such as a curved screen, that allows the user to experience content in a highly engaging way. This setting is used to display introductory and tutorial videos.

C641.name: Boat ride experience
C641.definition: A boat ride experience is a design element intended to give the user the feeling of being transported from one bank of a river to another. This feeling is implemented at the very start of the tour.

C642.name: 360-degree boat ride video
C642.definition: A 360-degree boat ride video is a specific type of video used to make the user feel as if they are actually traveling through a boat. This video facilitates the feeling of transport from the mainland to the island.

C643.name: Pre-processing
C643.definition: Pre-processing is the initial content processing performed on collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and quality of the user experience.

C644.name: Uniform illumination
C644.definition: Uniform illumination is the process of editing images to ensure that the lighting effect remains consistent across all captured images, even if they were taken at different times.

C645.name: 360-degree image
C645.definition: A 360-degree image is a type of image used to create scenes, allowing the user to travel and explore the environment from one image to the next.

C646.name: Ambient sound
C646.definition: Ambient sound refers to natural sounds, such as birds chirping or temple bells, that are integrated into the experience to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience.

C647.name: Virtual tablet
C647.definition: Virtual tablet is the main interface that provides users with navigation tools, access to information content, and a video player.

C648.name: Minimap
C648.definition: Minimap is a world-in-miniature type of support that provides a sense of orientation for a specific location. It aids navigation by reflecting the arrangement of 360-degree images.

C649.name: Dual map
C649.definition: Dual maps are a design technique that utilizes both a global map and a local map. This combination reduces clutter and provides clear navigation support.

C650.name: Orientation awareness
C650.definition: Orientation awareness is the ability to provide users with spatial orientation. The mini maps specifically provide dynamic orientation awareness to show users the direction they should move.

C651.name: Information icon
C651.definition: Information icon is a visual element that provides further details about a place when it is interacted with by the user, typically in the form of textual information.

C652.name: View interpolation
C652.definition: View interpolation is a technique that ensures smooth visual transition by blurring the boundaries between two images. This process allows the user to experience a smooth feeling when moving from one image to another.

C653.name: Virtual vehicle metaphor
C653.definition: Virtual vehicle metaphor is a 3D model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within a tour. This metaphor allows the user to explore an entire island, not just a single space.

C654.name: Ray casting interactions
C654.definition: Ray casting interactions allow users to operate a virtual vehicle by providing a direction of movement. The user can select a place to move, and the vehicle will accordingly move to that location.

C655.name: Selection-based locomotion technique
C655.definition: Selection-based locomotion technique is a method where the user selects a destination to initiate travel. This technique utilizes a pre-planned route rather than instantaneous movement or target selection.

C656.name: Route selection
C656.definition: Route selection is a travel technique where the user selects a destination. The system then selects a pre-planned route to facilitate the travel to that chosen destination.

C657.name: Video player
C657.definition: Video player is a component integrated into the tablet interface that allows users to access and view various types of cultural and ecological videos.

C658.name: 360-degree video
C658.definition: 360-degree video is a specific format of video content that can be accessed by the user within the system.

C659.name: Textual description
C659.definition: Textual description provides additional context about locations and significant spots, thereby enriching the user's understanding and engagement.

C660.name: Directional arrow
C660.definition: Directional arrow is a visual element added to the system that guides users toward specific points of interest.

C661.name: Controlled navigation technique
C661.definition: Controlled navigation technique is a method implemented to allow users to navigate or teleport using a joystick. This technique reduces abrupt movements that are known to cause discomfort.

C662.name: Usability evaluation
C662.definition: Usability evaluation is a process used to assess extended reality systems. It determines whether the system successfully meets the established design goals from the point of view of the user.

C663.name: User requirement gathering
C663.definition: User requirement gathering is the process of determining what a user needs from a system, which involves utilizing various data collection and analysis techniques. This process was applied to the Majuli Island virtual tour design case study.

C664.name: Designing the experience
C664.definition: Designing the experience is the process of creating the overall user experience based on the requirements that were gathered. This stage follows the requirement gathering phase.

C665.name: Implementation
C665.definition: Implementation is the final stage of the development process, focusing on how the XR system is put into practice. This stage follows the discussion of requirement gathering and design.

C666.name: System implementation
C666.definition: System implementation is the process of implementing the design ideas that were formulated based on the requirements. This is one of the concepts discussed in the lecture.

C667.name: Prototyping techniques
C667.definition: Prototyping techniques are methods used specifically for collecting feedback on the usability of design ideas. These techniques facilitate both quick prototyping and quick evaluation of the design.

C668.name: Horizontal prototype
C668.definition: Horizontal prototype is a type of prototype that focuses on the breadth of features. Low fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for creating this type of prototype.

C669.name: Vertical prototype
C669.definition: Vertical prototype is a representation created using a series of sketches. This type of prototype depicts the interaction flow and depth of the system.

C670.name: Low-fidelity prototype
C670.definition: Low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, meaning no programming or computer is required. These prototypes are typically constructed using simple materials like paper, cardboard, or wood.

C671.name: Interface sketch
C671.definition: Interface sketch is a drawing that depicts the major components of an interface and provides a way to envision its appearance. These sketches allow users to provide feedback on an idea before any formal development begins.

C672.name: Horizontal prototyping
C672.definition: Horizontal prototyping is primarily associated with low-fidelity approaches and is used to brainstorm alternative designs. This method helps gather user responses and feedback on the overall idea and usability.

C673.name: Vertical prototyping
C673.definition: Vertical prototyping is an approach that can be implemented using a low-fidelity method, even though it is not primarily associated with it. This method allows for the implementation of specific features or functions within the prototype.

C674.name: Storyboarding
C674.definition: Storyboarding is a series of sketches used to represent interaction. Storyboarding captures the sequence of actions required from the user to complete a specific task.

C675.name: Keyframe
C675.definition: Keyframe is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time. Each keyframe shows a specific instance of how the screen appears to the user during the execution of a task.

C676.name: Low fidelity approach
C676.definition: Low fidelity approach is a prototyping method that does not rely on computers, allowing for creation using simple media like paper. This method is primarily meant for creating horizontal prototypes.

C677.name: Medium fidelity approach
C677.definition: Medium fidelity approach is a prototyping method that uses a computer to create simple prototypes. These prototypes can be utilized to build either horizontal or vertical prototypes.

C678.name: High fidelity approach
C678.definition: High fidelity approach is a prototyping method where prototypes are created using computer programs. This process is effectively actual software development, making it more sophisticated and requiring skilled programmers.

C679.name: Wizard of Oz approach
C679.definition: Wizard of Oz approach is a prototyping technique where a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer. In reality, an unseen human operator, known as the wizard, controls the computer and returns the results to the subject.

C680.name: Throwaway prototypes
