C680.definition: Throwaway prototypes are prototypes used for a quick evaluation and are subsequently discarded. These prototypes are ideally low fidelity, such as paper sketches, because they are inexpensive and fast to create.

C681.name: Incremental prototypes
C681.definition: Incremental prototypes involve designing the system into separate units or modules. Each unit is prototyped and tested individually before being integrated into the complete system.

C682.name: Evolutionary prototypes
C682.definition: Evolutionary prototypes start with a simpler version of the whole system, which is then tested and refined. Functionalities are progressively added to evolve the prototype into the final product.

C683.name: Expert evaluation
C683.definition: Expert evaluation is a technique used for quick and cheap evaluation of prototypes. It is typically performed at an early stage of the design process without requiring significant time or resources.

C684.name: Evaluation team
C684.definition: Evaluation team is the group responsible for performing the evaluation of the prototype. This team may consist of the design team itself, skilled designers, or optionally, a few end users.

C685.name: Usability issues
C685.definition: Usability issues are a list of problems that are perceived by the evaluator during the testing process. These issues are compiled from individual reports to create a final list.

C686.name: Cognitive walkthrough
C686.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a usability inspection method used to identify usability problems by inspecting a prototype. This technique requires evaluators to perform tasks using the prototype while answering specific questions about the interaction.

C687.name: Storyboard
C687.definition: Storyboard is a series of sketches that depicts the changes of the screen after each interaction within a prototype. Essentially, each prototype created for this purpose functions as a storyboard.

C688.name: Scenario
C688.definition: Scenario is a task description that evaluators use to perform tasks supported in the prototype. This scenario helps define the specific goal the user is trying to achieve using the interface.

C689.name: Heuristic evaluation
C689.definition: Heuristic evaluation is a technique where evaluators check a design prototype against a list of heuristics. Evaluators report findings on whether each heuristic is followed or violated, and provide reasons for any violations.

C690.name: Recognition rather than recall
C690.definition: Recognition rather than recall is a principle stating that users should recognize necessary actions from elements rather than being forced to remember information to perform a task.

C691.name: User evaluation
C691.definition: User evaluation is a quick feedback technique that requires involving users directly to gather information. This method is often called evaluation with self-reports, where feedback is collected using rating scales.

C692.name: Expert evaluation technique
C692.definition: Expert evaluation technique is a method used to quickly assess prototypes, where the involvement of users is optional. These techniques rely on specialized knowledge to evaluate the design.

C693.name: Likert scale
C693.definition: Likert scale is a well-known rating scale used to collect user feedback by asking them to rate statements or questions. Users provide a rating on this scale, such as a three-point or seven-point scale.

C694.name: System Usability Scale
C694.definition: System Usability Scale (SUS) is a popular post-session questionnaire designed to measure the overall usability of a system. This questionnaire consists of 10 statements, which are rated on a 5-point agreement scale.

C695.name: Virtual reality sickness questionnaire
C695.definition: Virtual reality sickness questionnaire (VRSQ) is a relevant questionnaire used for evaluating experiences within virtual reality. It is particularly useful when assessing VR experiences utilizing Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs).

C696.name: Cyber sickness questionnaire
C696.definition: Cyber sickness questionnaire (CSQ) is a relevant questionnaire designed to assess cyber sickness. It is one of the specific tools used for measuring discomfort in immersive experiences.

C697.name: Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
C697.definition: Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MSSQ) is a tool used to measure a person's susceptibility to motion sickness. It is one of several questionnaires designed to assess specific conditions related to motion sickness.

C698.name: 360-degree image
C698.definition: 360-degree image is a type of visual content used in VR tours that allows the user to view a complete, immersive panoramic scene. Each image represents a specific location within the virtual environment.

C699.name: Ray casting-based selection method
C699.definition: Ray casting-based selection method is a mechanism used to allow the user to make selections on the start screen. This method determines which object the user is pointing at in the virtual space.

C700.name: Empirical evaluation
C700.definition: Empirical evaluation is a detailed method of testing a system's usability. This type of evaluation goes beyond quick or cheap methods to provide in-depth user feedback.

C701.name: Empirical study
C701.definition: Empirical study is a form of research used in the stage of evaluation. This type of study is known in several forms, such as usability study or empirical research.

C702.name: Fully implemented system
C702.definition: Fully implemented system is a complete version of the system that is required for conclusive usability evaluation. This type of evaluation cannot be performed on prototypes.

C703.name: Controlled experiment
C703.definition: Controlled experiment is a method that must be performed to collect user behavioral data. This data is then analyzed to reach a conclusion about the overall system's usability.

C704.name: Usability study
C704.definition: Usability study is a specific type of controlled experiment used in this context to evaluate how well a system functions for a user. This process allows researchers to assess the overall usability aspects of a system.

C705.name: Identification of research questions
C705.definition: Identification of research questions is the initial stage of empirical research where specific questions are formulated to guide the investigation and seek answers. These questions define the scope of the research that needs to be performed.

C706.name: Determination of variables
C706.definition: Determination of variables is the second stage of the process, requiring the identification of different types of variables after the research questions have been formulated. Identifying these variables is necessary to successfully design and execute a controlled experiment.

C707.name: Design of experiment
C707.definition: Design of experiment is the crucial third stage, involving both the design of the experiment and the subsequent collection of data through the execution of that design. This stage is considered the core of the process where data collection is planned.

C708.name: Analysis of the data
C708.definition: Analysis of the data is the final, rigorous stage where data is scientifically and objectively analyzed. This process ensures that the resulting conclusion about the system's usability is reliable.

C709.name: Research question
C709.definition: Research question is the fundamental query that guides an empirical study. It is framed to determine the specific knowledge or answer that the experiment aims to find.

C710.name: Testable question
C710.definition: Testable question is a research question that allows for the collection of objective data through a controlled study. These questions can be objectively verified or falsified.

C711.name: Untestable question
C711.definition: Untestable question is a research question that cannot be objectively tested through a controlled experiment. These questions rely purely on subjective interpretation and feedback.

C712.name: Objective data
C712.definition: Objective data is information that can be measured factually and is not influenced by personal feelings or interpretations. This data allows for definitive and reliable conclusions.

C713.name: Subjective feedback
C713.definition: Subjective feedback is information derived from a user's personal opinion or interpretation of a system. This type of feedback is prone to individual bias and is difficult to use for definitive scientific conclusions.

C714.name: Independent variable
C714.definition: Independent variable is a variable that is controlled by the researcher during an experiment. These variables are manipulated to observe their effect on other variables.

C715.name: Factor
C715.definition: Factor is a term used interchangeably with independent variable. It represents the variable that is controlled and manipulated during an experiment.

C716.name: Level
C716.definition: Level is the specific value assigned to a variable or factor. These values define the different conditions of the variable being tested.

C717.name: Dependent variable
C717.definition: Dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on the independent variable or its levels. It is the variable that is measured to see if it changes based on the manipulation.

C718.name: Test condition
C718.definition: Test condition is created by combining the factors with their assigned levels. These conditions define the specific setup required for running the experiment.

C719.name: Empirical
C719.definition: Empirical means observation in the real world of real users.

C720.name: Research question framing
C720.definition: Research question framing is the process of converting broad, generalizable questions that are untestable into multiple testable research questions. These testable questions allow for the collection of objective data, which can then be combined to draw conclusions about the original untestable goals

C721.name: Testable research question
C721.definition: A testable research question is a specific question, such as 'which one is faster?', that has been identified for the empirical study. This question guides the entire evaluation process.

C722.name: User profile
C722.definition: User profile is a careful consideration used when choosing a subset of participants for an experiment. It involves defining the user based on well-defined characteristics and entries.

C723.name: Homogeneous user group
C723.definition: A homogeneous user group is a collection of users that generally share similarities in their backgrounds. These similarities can include educational, socio-economic, or cultural backgrounds.

C724.name: Number of participants
C724.definition: Number of participants refers to the quantity of users engaged in an empirical study, which must be sufficient to draw reliable conclusions. Generally, using between 12 and 25 participants is considered adequate for reliable data collection.

C725.name: Representative task
C725.definition: Representative task is a specific task chosen for an experiment that reflects the activities most frequently used by the potential user group when the interface is deployed in practice. These tasks are selected based on certain metrics and measures to ensure the collected data is reliable.

C726.name: Task performance data
C726.definition: Task performance data is the information collected when participants carry out tasks during an experiment. This data is intended to be mostly objective and is analyzed to reach a conclusion about the interface.

C727.name: Task
C727.definition: Task is an activity that participants are asked to perform during the experiment. The selection of appropriate tasks is crucial because otherwise, the observed data may not be useful for evaluation.

C728.name: Within-subject design
C728.definition: Within-subject design is a study design where every participant performs tasks corresponding to all test conditions. This means all participants are given every task in the experiment.

C729.name: Between-subjects design
C729.definition: Between-subjects design is a study where tasks are distributed among different participants. In this design, not every participant performs all the tasks corresponding to all test conditions.

C730.name: Practice effect
C730.definition: The practice effect is a phenomenon where a user's performance improves simply because they have practiced the tasks. This improvement is due to the inherent human nature of acquiring skills while practicing.

C731.name: Confounding variable
C731.definition: A confounding variable is a factor that mixes or confuses the analysis of an experiment. This makes it difficult to determine whether observed performance changes are due to the interface or due to natural skill acquisition.

C732.name: Latin square design
C732.definition: A Latin square design is a systematic method of varying the sequence of tasks assigned to each participant. This variation is used to nullify the effect of the practice effect.

C733.name: Data analysis
C733.definition: Data analysis is the main purpose of the final stage of system implementation, where collected data is processed to determine its reliability before any conclusions are drawn.

C734.name: Statistical significance
C734.definition: Statistical significance is a test used to determine if collected data is reliable, indicating whether observed results are due to the inherent nature of the design or merely due to chance.

C735.name: Mean or average
C735.definition: Mean or average is a starting statistic used in data processing, representing the average of a group of data items within a sample.

C736.name: Parametric tests
C736.definition: Parametric tests are a group of statistical tests used when the input data meets specific assumptions about the population distribution. These tests are often used when dealing with continuous data.

C737.name: Non-parametric tests
C737.definition: Non-parametric tests are a group of statistical tests used when the data does not meet the assumptions required by parametric tests. These tests are often used with nominal or categorical scales of measurement.

C738.name: Paired sample T test
C738.definition: Paired sample T test is a specific statistical test used for within-subject designs to compare the means of two related groups. This test helps determine if the difference between the two means is statistically significant.

C739.name: Quick evaluation
C739.definition: Quick evaluation is a stage of the design prototype evaluation cycle that is performed after the prototype is implemented. This evaluation does not require the full system to be ready.

C740.name: Empirical study
C740.definition: Empirical study is the process of collecting data from end users by means of a controlled experiment, often utilizing questionnaires for data collection.

C741.name: Usability
C741.definition: Usability is a point of view used to measure certain aspects of the system.

C742.name: Symptoms of cyber sickness
C742.definition: Symptoms of cyber sickness are physical or psychological responses that are analyzed alongside participant responses to identify potential areas for improvement in the virtual tour.

C743.name: QEP questionnaire
C743.definition: QEP questionnaire is a revised version of the presence questionnaire proposed in 2004. It is used specifically for the measure of presence.

C744.name: Presence questionnaire
C744.definition: Presence questionnaire is a standard questionnaire designed to measure the psychological state of presence. A revised version of this questionnaire was proposed in 2004.

C745.name: Previous presence questionnaire
C745.definition: Previous presence questionnaire (QEP) is a specific questionnaire used to assess the user's prior experience with a location. It utilizes a Likert scale to gauge the correspondence between real and virtual visits.

C746.name: Familiarity bias
C746.definition: Familiarity bias is a potential issue where participants who are already familiar with VR systems produce results different from those who are not. This bias can lead to incorrect conclusions based on the analysis of the obtained data.

C747.name: Pre-exposure assessment
C747.definition: Pre-exposure assessment is a measurement conducted before the user is exposed to the system. This assessment serves to establish a baseline data point for comparison after the user has interacted with the system.

C748.name: Presence questionnaire (QEP questionnaire)
C748.definition: Presence questionnaire (QEP questionnaire) is a measure participants fill out at the end of the session. This questionnaire assesses the user's subjective sense of being present within the virtual environment.

C749.name: Involvement
C749.definition: Involvement is one of the several items that constitute the measure of presence. It is one of the factors used to rate the user experience within the system.

C750.name: Interface quality
C750.definition: Interface quality is one of the several items that make up the measure of presence. It relates to how well the user interacts with the system.

C751.name: Adaptation or immersion
C751.definition: Adaptation or immersion is one of the several items that makes up the measure of presence. It relates to how the user adjusts to or is absorbed by the virtual environment.

C752.name: Visual fidelity
C752.definition: Visual fidelity is one of the several items that makes up the measure of presence. It refers to the quality of the visual representation provided by the system.

C753.name: Good presence
C753.definition: Good presence is a quality where the system successfully convinces users that the digital environment is close to reality. This indicates a high level of immersion and realism in the virtual experience.

C754.name: Welch t-test
C754.definition: Welch t-test is a specific statistical test used to reveal a significant difference between groups of users. This test is employed when comparing data between experienced and inexperienced users.

C755.name: SSQ Questionnaire (Sickness Questionnaire)
C755.definition: SSQ Questionnaire (Sickness Questionnaire) is the specific instrument used to collect data and measure the severity of cyber sickness in both pre and post exposure situations.

C756.name: Wilcoxon signed rank test
C756.definition: Wilcoxon signed rank test is a statistical significance test performed to determine if the observed differences between pre and post exposure scores are statistically significant.

C757.name: Requirement gathering
C757.definition: Requirement gathering is the initial stage where functional and non-functional requirements are collected from both end users and clients. Different methods, such as contextual inquiry, may be used to collect these requirements.

C758.name: Empirical study
C758.definition: Empirical study is a method used to estimate usability by identifying participants and gathering their time. This study helps determine if there are still gaps in the system's usability.

C759.name: Black box testing
C759.definition: Black box testing is a systematic and structured way of testing the system. This method focuses on the system's functionality without needing to know its internal structure.

C760.name: White box testing
C760.definition: White box testing is a systematic and structured way of testing the system. This method involves examining the internal workings of the system.

C761.name: Feasibility study report
C761.definition: Feasibility study report is a document required during the feasibility study stage. This report assesses whether a proposed project is viable.

C762.name: Design document
C762.definition: Design document is a document required during the design phase. It details both the interface design and the code design to aid understanding and debugging.

C763.name: Usability study report
C763.definition: Usability study report is a document created after usability testing. This report evaluates how easy the system is for users to operate.

C764.name: Agile development framework
C764.definition: Agile development framework is a method that encourages fast development and quick turnaround of projects. This framework eliminates unnecessary documentation and focuses on delivering features incrementally.

C765.name: Iteration
C765.definition: Iteration, also known as a sprint, is the development cycle that includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery. This cycle is typically short, lasting four to six weeks.

C766.name: Conceptualization
C766.definition: Conceptualization is an initial stage of the process flow that roughly refers to the physical feasibility study. This stage also involves the gathering of requirements.

C767.name: Inception
C767.definition: Inception is an initial stage that involves the creation of the team and the arrangement of necessary funds and resources. This stage, along with conceptualization, refers to requirement gathering.

C768.name: Release
C768.definition: Release is a stage in the process flow that includes testing, training, and documentation. This stage follows the development cycle and precedes production.

C769.name: Prototype-evaluate
C769.definition: Prototype-evaluate is the part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle that focuses on how to build and evaluate prototypes.

C770.name: Agile development method
C770.definition: Agile development method is a practical way of building interactive systems when compared to standard system development life cycles.

C771.name: Optimization
C771.definition: Optimization is the process of optimizing both the system requirements and the user experience.

C772.name: Usability
C772.definition: Usability is a quality that is finally evaluated during the empirical evaluation process.

C773.name: Optimizing VR Navigation Experience
C773.definition: Optimizing VR Navigation Experience is the new topic of the lecture, focusing on how to improve the navigation experience within Virtual Reality.

C774.name: Optimized experience (psychophysiological experience optimization)
C774.definition: Optimized experience (psychophysiological experience optimization) is one of the two perspectives used to view optimization in VR. This perspective focuses on the user's psychophysiological experience.

C775.name: Optimized resource utilization (technological optimization)
C775.definition: Optimized resource utilization (technological optimization) is the second perspective for discussing optimization in VR. This perspective relates to the resource requirement of the system.

C776.name: Experience optimization
C776.definition: Experience optimization is the process of designing an experience to minimize cyber sickness or the possibility of its induction while using a system. This process is considered an optimization problem.

C777.name: Resource optimization
C777.definition: Resource optimization is the effort to build systems that minimize resource requirements in XR or VR. This must be done while ensuring that the immersive experience is not compromised.

C778.name: Internal factors
C778.definition: Internal factors are elements related to the user themselves that are primarily responsible for cyber sickness. These factors include the user's age, gender, physical condition, and emotional condition.

C779.name: External factors
C779.definition: External factors are elements outside of the user that can induce cyber sickness. These factors are broadly divided into hardware and VR content categories.

C780.name: Hardware factors
C780.definition: Hardware factors are external elements related to the physical equipment used in VR that are considered responsible for cyber sickness. These factors include display resolution, latency, and type of input.

C781.name: Virtual locomotion techniques
C781.definition: Virtual locomotion techniques are methods used to navigate within a virtual reality world. These techniques allow a user to perform a virtual reality tour in the virtual environment.

C782.name: User-controlled virtual tours
C782.definition: System-controlled virtual tours are tours where the application or system dictates the user's travel within the VR environment. The user's movement and navigation are guided by the system itself, often following a predetermined path.

C783.name: System-controlled tour
C783.definition: System-controlled tour is a type of tour where the system manages the navigation and movement, providing the user with an effortless experience and reduced cognitive demands. System-controlled tours are the focus of this lecture segment.

C784.name: Cognitive demand
C784.definition: Cognitive demand is the mental effort required from the user, which is reduced when the system takes over decision-making tasks such as determining how or which way to move. Reduced cognitive demands allow the user to concentrate more on the experience itself.

C785.name: Realistic walking experience
C785.definition: Realistic walking experience is a navigation state where the user forgets the system control, causing the difference between the realistic and unrealistic environment to vanish in the user's mind. This experience is the objective of using a system-controlled tool.

C786.name: Optic flow
C786.definition: Optic flow is the speed of change of the scene, which is used to simulate movement in a virtual world. This speed determines how the user perceives movement by observing the surroundings.

C787.name: VR experience optimization
C787.definition: VR experience optimization is the process of improving the quality of the virtual reality experience. This concept is essentially equated with psychophysiological optimization.

C788.name: Natural walking experience
C788.definition: Natural walking experience is the desired outcome of the optimization effort. It involves creating a realistic walking experience within the VR world, particularly in a system-controlled tour.

C789.name: Realistic walking behavior model
C789.definition: Realistic walking behavior model is a model of natural walking behavior that can be utilized to address concerns regarding VR navigation. This model is specifically designed for system-controlled VR navigation.

C790.name: VR navigation experience
C790.definition: VR navigation experience is the process of moving within a Virtual Reality environment that requires optimization. The goal of optimization is to ensure a realistic walking experience for the user.

C791.name: Speed estimation model
C791.definition: Speed estimation model is a proposed model designed to gather real-life working data when a user moves from one point to another.

C792.name: Walking behavior
C792.definition: Walking behavior is the manner in which a user moves, which is affected by factors such as height.

C793.name: Photograph-clicking task
C793.definition: Photograph-clicking task is an assigned activity where the user stops at a painting to click a photo, ensuring they stop after walking a predefined distance.

C794.name: Instantaneous step frequency
C794.definition: Instantaneous step frequency is the rate of steps taken by the user, which is represented as a function of distance. This frequency is similar or related to the actual speed.

C795.name: Step
C795.definition: A step is defined as the interval between one foot strike and the next foot strike on the ground. This interval signifies the occurrence of a step.

C796.name: Velocity
C796.definition: Velocity is the speed of the user, which the study tracked to observe how it changes over time during walking. The user's velocity was observed to increase gradually, reach a maximum, and then decrease before stopping.

C797.name: Slow in slow out pattern
C797.definition: Slow in slow out pattern is a specific pattern observed in the study, characterized by a change in speed that starts slowly, accelerates, remains constant, and then slows down.

C798.name: Fourier series
C798.definition: Fourier series is a mathematical series that approximates any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision by using weighted terms.

C799.name: Perceived speed
C799.definition: Perceived speed is the rate of movement that an individual experiences visually, which may not be the same as the actual physical speed of movement.

C800.name: Visual gain
C800.definition: Visual gain is a factor multiplied by the actual speed to compute the desired visual speed. This factor is used to obtain a different speed that is perceived as natural.

C801.name: Actual visual speed
C801.definition: Actual visual speed is the speed obtained by multiplying the instantaneous speed by the visual gain. This resulting speed is what is perceived as natural.

C802.name: Actual speed
C802.definition: Actual speed is the speed at which the user is physically moving, which is related to the instantaneous step frequency. This speed is represented by a specific mathematical formulation.

C803.name: CISO pattern
C803.definition: CISO pattern is a specific pattern revealed by studies that is similar to the Fourier transform of sinusoidal waveforms. This pattern allows for the computation of the actual speed.

C804.name: Instantaneous speed
C804.definition: Instantaneous speed is the natural walking speed model utilized in the experiment. This speed model is contrasted with a constant speed experience.

C805.name: Natural walking behavior
C805.definition: Natural walking behavior is the desired perception that the user experiences when moving through the virtual environment. This behavior is achieved by computing natural walking behavior and multiplying it by a visual gain factor.

C806.name: Empirical study
C806.definition: Empirical study is a stage of the model evaluation process used to confirm whether a model enhances perceived realism compared to a constant average speed. The purpose of this study was to confirm the model's effectiveness.

C807.name: Perceived realism
C807.definition: Perceived realism is the measure of how real the user experiences the virtual environment to be. The study aimed to confirm whether the usage of the model enhances this perceived realism.

C808.name: Realistic walking speed model
C808.definition: Realistic walking speed model is a model designed for system-controlled virtual reality tools. Its primary purpose is to maximize the presence of the user.

C809.name: Level of realism
C809.definition: Level of realism refers to the quality of the experience that is judged by the user. This level is one of the requirements that the developed model must meet.

C810.name: Preference for such a model
C810.definition: Preference for such a model refers to the user's specific desires regarding the design of the model. The developed model must satisfy this user preference.

C811.name: Exposure duration
C811.definition: Duration of exposure refers to the total time a user spends experiencing a virtual tour. This duration is the primary variable that the optimization process seeks to improve.

C812.name: Perceived instantaneous walking speed
C812.definition: Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the walking speed as experienced by the user, which is represented by the visual gain into the actual instantaneous speed. This speed is represented in a specific mathematical form.

C813.name: Teleportation-type movement
C813.definition: Teleportation-type movement is a method of navigation where the speed is at its maximum. This results in instantaneous movement occurring between two specific points.

C814.name: Mental map
C814.definition: A mental map is a concept that users build in the virtual world. This map is essential for the user's ability to perform wayfinding activities.

C815.name: Interaction time
C815.definition: Interaction time is the specific duration of time required for a user to interact with the virtual objects. This time can be ignored in entirely system-controlled VR tools.

C816.name: Points of interest
C816.definition: Points of interest are the nodes in the graph that represent specific locations within the virtual world. These are the locations that the optimized path must cover.

C817.name: Semi-interactive tour
C817.definition: A semi-interactive tour is a virtual tour design that imposes a limit on the amount of time a user can spend interacting at any single point of interest. This time limit is used to optimize the overall duration of the experience.

C818.name: System-controlled VR tool
C818.definition: A system-controlled VR tool is a virtual reality application where the movement or travel between points is managed automatically by the system. In this scenario, the interaction time can be disregarded.

C819.name: Optimum path
C819.definition: Optimum path is the most efficient route designed to meet a specific goal within the virtual tour. This path either ensures all points of interest are visited in minimum time or maximizes the number of points visited within a fixed time.

C820.name: Weighted graph
C820.definition: Weighted graph is a representation of the virtual world where the connections between points of interest are assigned numerical values. These weights typically denote the distance between the connected points.

C821.name: Vertex
C821.definition: Vertex is a node in the graph that represents a specific point of interest within the virtual world. Each point of interest is assumed to be a vertex in the graph structure.

C822.name: Edge weight
C822.definition: Edge weight is the value assigned to a connection between two vertices, representing the cost or distance of traveling between them. This weight is calculated using the Euclidean distance if a direct path exists, or a very large number if no direct path is available.

C823.name: Complete graph
C823.definition: Complete graph is a graph structure where every vertex is directly connected to every other vertex. This structure is created by adding hypothetical edges to the original graph.

C824.name: Natural walking speed
C824.definition: Natural walking speed is the foundational model used to calculate the time required to travel between connected points. This model assumes a realistic human gait for the movement.

C825.name: Actual instantaneous walking speed
C825.definition: Actual instantaneous walking speed is the realistic speed of the user at any given moment, represented by the variable V act. This speed is derived from the user's step frequency and height.

C826.name: Total travel time
C826.definition: Total travel time is the cumulative time required to traverse a distance, which is found by taking an integral of the instantaneous time element over the total distance. This calculation determines the time between two connected nodes.

C827.name: Travel time estimate tau D
C827.definition: Travel time estimate tau D is the final computed value for the time between two directly connected vertices. This estimate is derived after applying various mathematical simplifications and Fourier series expansions.

C828.name: Travelling salesman problem
C828.definition: The Travelling salesman problem is a problem that seeks the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node within a complete graph.

C829.name: Hamiltonian path
C829.definition: A Hamiltonian path is a path within a graph that covers all nodes, where each node is visited exactly once.

C830.name: Hypothetical edge
C830.definition: A hypothetical edge is an introduced edge used for computation when two vertices lack a direct connection in the original graph.

C831.name: Modified edge weight
C831.definition: The modified edge weight is the weight between two nodes, defined as the Euclidean distance if they are directly connected, or the shortest path length if they are not.

C832.name: Shortest path
C832.definition: Shortest path is the optimal route between two vertices in the original graph. This path is used to replace any hypothetical edges found in the TSP solver's output.

C833.name: Travel time
C833.definition: Travel time is the specific weight assigned to an edge in the modified graph. This weight represents the actual time taken to travel from one vertex to another.

C834.name: Graph theoretic problem
C834.definition: Graph theoretic problem is the method of converting the virtual world into a graph structure. This structure uses points of interest as nodes and weighted edges representing the distance between them.

C835.name: Cybersickness time threshold
C835.definition: Cybersickness time threshold is the maximum time limit that, if exceeded, increases the possibility of cybersickness. The algorithm must ensure the calculated minimum time remains below this threshold.

C836.name: Time threshold
C836.definition: Time threshold is the maximum allowed time limit within which a path must be completed. This constraint dictates which paths are viable for the problem statement.

C837.name: Points of interest
C837.definition: Points of interest are specific locations or vertices within the virtual world. The objective of the second optimization approach is to cover the maximum number of these points.

C838.name: Importance function
C838.definition: Importance function is a function (f, v) that assigns a positive real number to every vertex or point of interest. This number indicates the importance of that specific vertex.

C839.name: Node importance
C839.definition: Node importance is the measure of how important a specific node is, captured as a positive real number. A higher value of this number signifies a higher importance.

C840.name: Total importance
C840.definition: Total importance is the aggregated measure of a given path. This value is calculated by summing the individual importance of every node within that path.

C841.name: Path
C841.definition: Path is a sequence of nodes, denoted as P, that contains nodes from V1 to Vn. This path is the route being evaluated for optimization.

C842.name: Waiting time
C842.definition: Waiting time is the time required by a user to inspect or interact with a particular object located at a node. This value represents the maximum time a user needs to spend at that point of interest.

C843.name: Waiting time function
C843.definition: The waiting time function is a defined function that maps every node to a real positive number. This number indicates the maximum time required for a user to inspect or interact with the object at that node.

C844.name: Total waiting time
C844.definition: Total waiting time is calculated by summing the individual waiting times for all nodes that constitute a specific path. This calculation is performed in a manner similar to calculating total importance.

C845.name: Vehicle routing problem
C845.definition: Vehicle routing problem (VRP) is a well-known problem in operations research that serves as the basis for the problem being solved in this lecture.

C846.name: VRP with profit
C846.definition: VRP with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP) where the goal is to maximize profit within given time constraints.

C847.name: Cybersickness
C847.definition: Cybersickness is a condition that may occur when a user's exposure time exceeds a specific time threshold.

C848.name: Optimal path P
C848.definition: Optimal path P is the desired output of the algorithm, representing a route that maximizes the importance (F) of visited nodes while ensuring the total exposure time remains below a specified threshold.

C849.name: VRPP solver
C849.definition: VRPP solver is a specialized computational tool used to determine the optimal path by taking the final modified graph, node importance values, and waiting times as input.

C850.name: Natural walking model
C850.definition: Natural walking model is a method used to compute the travel time between nodes, ensuring that the resulting travel duration provides a realistic experience.

C851.name: Cyber sickness issues
C851.definition: Cyber sickness issues are concerns related to virtual reality that may be induced if the time spent in the environment is too large. These issues are a primary concern that optimization strategies must address.

C852.name: Optimal path approach
C852.definition: Optimal path approach is a method for identifying a route in a virtual world that allows the user to explore every point of interest in the shortest possible time. This approach seeks to cover all points of interest in minimum duration.

C853.name: Optimal path under time constraint
C853.definition: Optimal path under time constraint is a method where the user must cover a path that maximizes the number of important points of interest within a predefined time threshold. This constraint sets an upper limit on the duration of the virtual tour.

C854.name: Points of interest
C854.definition: Points of interest are specific locations that are identified and used as nodes in the graph formulation for pathfinding. These locations are critical for determining the optimal route.

C855.name: Graph theoretic form
C855.definition: Graph theoretic form is the mathematical structure used to model a practical problem so that optimization approaches can be applied to it. This form allows the theoretical concepts to be put into practice.

C856.name: Walking-based exploration
C856.definition: Walking-based exploration is a method of virtual tour where the user navigates the virtual environment by simulating natural walking movements. This method is used to achieve a realistic experience within the virtual world.

C857.name: Graph
C857.definition: Graph is a structure formulated to represent connections between nodes, where the distance between nodes is measured. This structure allows algorithms to determine optimal paths.

C858.name: Contextual inquiry
C858.definition: Contextual inquiry is a field study method used to observe people's travel behavior and gather information about places of importance in their natural environment. This method involves observing users in situ and talking to local people for clarity.

C859.name: Euclidean distance
C859.definition: Euclidean distance is a method used to calculate the straight-line distance between two points. This calculated distance is then used as the weight for the edges connecting those points in the graph.

C860.name: Weight
C860.definition: Weight is the value assigned to an edge or between nodes, which represents either the measured distance or the relative importance of the connection. This value is used by algorithms to calculate the most efficient path.

C861.name: Resource optimization
C861.definition: Resource optimization is the second type of optimization discussed in XR. It focuses on managing the necessary resources for an immersive experience.

C862.name: Resource optimization
C862.definition: Resource optimization is an objective in extended reality that involves building systems to minimize the requirement of resources. This is done without compromising the user experience, which means maximizing the experience.

C863.name: Resource requirements
C863.definition: Resource requirements are the necessary resources that extended reality (XR), particularly virtual reality (VR), needs to operate. Systems must be built to minimize these requirements while simultaneously optimizing the experience.

C864.name: Resource
C864.definition: Resource, in the context of Virtual Reality, refers to the hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure required for the system. This includes specific components like input devices, processing devices, output devices, and various types of infrastructure.

C865.name: Digital infrastructure
C865.definition: Digital infrastructure refers to the network-related components necessary for a setup. This includes network gears, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

C866.name: Physical infrastructure
C866.definition: Physical infrastructure refers to the tangible elements supporting a setup. This includes rooms, furniture, and the supply of electricity.

C867.name: Client end
C867.definition: Client end refers to the location where the user has direct access to the hardware, making it the primary focus for resource optimization. This is the physical point where the user experiences the virtual reality system.

C868.name: Hardware resources
C868.definition: Hardware resource refers to the physical components that are being focused on for optimization at the client end. Understanding these resources is necessary to understand the 'why' of optimization.

C869.name: Object
C869.definition: An object is a geometric shape that can be part of a specific item or part of the overall interface. Objects include the main item and interface elements like menus or icons.

C870.name: Image
C870.definition: An image is the entire thing displayed on the screen, which is not limited to just the main object. This whole display is comprised of geometric shapes, and each shape has an attached color.

C871.name: Synthesis
C871.definition: Synthesis is the process of combining individual parts to form a complete and realistic image. This process addresses how parts are put together to create a full scene.

C872.name: Generic graphics system
C872.definition: Generic graphics system is a framework that outlines the major components and basic terms needed to understand the process of rendering. This system provides the overall structure for image generation.

C873.name: Display controller
C873.definition: Display controller generates the image in a digital format, which consists of strings of zeros and ones. Display controller outputs this representation of the image in binary form.

C874.name: Video memory
C874.definition: Video memory is a major component used for storing data that is sent by the display controller. This stored data is subsequently utilized by the video controller.

C875.name: Video controller
C875.definition: Video controller converts the digital image stored in the video memory into analog voltages. Video controller controls the mechanism that activates the pixels on the display screen.

C876.name: Graphics card
C876.definition: Graphics card is a dedicated component of a computer designed to handle rendering-related computations. It typically comprises a Graphics processing unit (GPU) and is responsible for processing visual data.

C877.name: Pixel
C877.definition: Pixel is a picture element that is arranged in a grid on a graphic display screen. Pixels are activated to emit light, which allows the viewer to perceive a colored image.

C878.name: Vector scan device
C878.definition: A vector scan device is a graphic device that renders an image by activating only selective pixels that represent continuous geometric primitives, such as lines or curves. This method assumes that focusing on the rendering of these primitives allows the whole image to be perceived.

C879.name: Raster scan device
C879.definition: Raster scan device is a display mechanism that renders images by following a left-to-right, top-to-bottom scanning manner. This sequential scanning causes the excitation of pixels to occur at different times across the screen.

C880.name: Raster scan displays
C880.definition: Raster scan displays are the type of display typically found in commercial products such as smartphones or televisions. These displays utilize a specific scanning method to render images.

C881.name: Frame buffer
C881.definition: The frame buffer is the video memory component of a raster scan system. It contains one memory location corresponding to each pixel, storing the intensity value for that pixel.

C882.name: Screen refreshing
C882.definition: Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels to counteract the natural decay of emitted light. This process ensures that the image remains uniform and stable even when the scene itself is not changing.

C883.name: Refresh rate
C883.definition: Refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on the screen. It is typically measured in hertz.

C884.name: Color display
C884.definition: Color display is a specific type of screen where each pixel contains more than one type of element. These elements are capable of emitting light with different intensities.

C885.name: Primary color
C885.definition: Primary color refers to the three fundamental colors—red, green, and blue—that are typically used by elements in a pixel. These colors are emitted with different intensities to represent a combination of colors.

C886.name: 3D graphics pipeline
C886.definition: 3D graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process that describes the computation flow. This process starts from the object representation and concludes with the rendering onto the pixel grid.

C887.name: Graphics pipeline
C887.definition: Graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process used to compute the values that are stored in the frame buffer. This process ultimately drives the display mechanism via the video controller.

C888.name: Display processor
C888.definition: Display processor is the component, which is part of the display controller, that is responsible for computing the necessary values in distinct stages. These values are real numbers stored in the framebuffer.

C889.name: Object representation
C889.definition: Object representation is the method used to structure computer-generated scenes, allowing for the depiction of objects that possess varying shapes, sizes, and characteristics.

C890.name: Modeling transformation
C890.definition: Modeling transformation is one of the stages in the graphics pipeline that involves transforming data from one coordinate system to another. This stage is part of the overall process of 3D graphics.

C891.name: Lighting stage
C891.definition: The lighting stage is the third stage where color is assigned to the constructed 3D scene. Assigning color is crucial because it makes the 3D nature of the scene more prominent and improves visual perception.

C892.name: Viewing transformation
C892.definition: Viewing transformation is a stage within the 3D graphics pipeline that involves transforming data from one coordinate system to another. This transformation is necessary for the rendering process.

C893.name: Scan conversion
C893.definition: Scan conversion is the fifth stage that transforms the continuous device coordinate space description into a discrete pixel grid description. This process maps the real-valued coordinates of the image points to the integer coordinates of the pixels.

C894.name: Balance
C894.definition: Balance is the necessary equilibrium between having a representation that captures all intricate details and ensuring that subsequent rendering computations are performed efficiently.

C895.name: Point sample rendering
C895.definition: Point sample rendering is a method where information is captured in the form of points on the scene, with each point carrying specific attributes. This process relies on real-world input sensors to generate a synthetic image of the scene.

C896.name: Boundary representation
C896.definition: Boundary representation is a technique where objects are defined by the surfaces that delineate the object's boundary. These surfaces can be either polygonal or curved.

C897.name: Spline representation
C897.definition: Spline representation is a higher-level method used to represent curved surfaces or curves, typically preferred by designers creating artificial environments. This representation uses several lower-degree polynomials to construct the complete curve.

C898.name: Object representation
C898.definition: Object representation is the first stage of the graphics pipeline. This stage involves representing the objects in the scene, though it does not involve intensity calculation.

C899.name: Viewing pipeline
C899.definition: Viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the graphics pipeline, which contains several sub-stages starting with viewing transformation.

C900.name: Clipping
C900.definition: Clipping is an operation that takes place in the 3D view coordinate system.

C901.name: Local coordinate system
C901.definition: Local coordinate system is a definition where an object is represented individually, allowing its position, dimension, and other properties to be defined relative to itself. Essentially, each object is thought of as having its own coordinate reference frame.

C902.name: World coordinate system
C902.definition: World coordinate system is a common coordinate system where multiple objects are assembled and defined together to construct a scene. This system allows objects, which are individually defined in their own local systems, to be placed together in a shared setting.

C903.name: Geometric transformation
C903.definition: Geometric transformation is the process of applying operations on an object's definition in local coordinates to transform it into the world or scene coordinate system. This stage is necessary to assemble multiple individually defined objects into a cohesive scene.

C904.name: Basic transformation
C904.definition: Basic transformation refers to the fundamental operations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing, that constitute the building blocks of all geometric transformations. Combinations of these basic operations can be used to create any required transformation for scene construction.

C905.name: Composite transformation matrix
C905.definition: Composite transformation matrix is a single matrix obtained by combining multiple basic transformations into one. This matrix is used when an object requires several operations, such as scaling and translation, to be moved from its local to the world coordinate system.

C906.name: Lighting model
C906.definition: Lighting model is a method used in computer graphics to simulate the process of light reflection and compute the color of a surface point. Lighting models involve a higher degree of computation compared to shading models.

C907.name: Shading model
C907.definition: Shading model is an approximation of color assignment that relies on lighting models. Shading models are designed to reduce computational requirements without significantly compromising the quality of the visual experience.

C908.name: Color computation
C908.definition: Color computation is the process of assigning colors to objects within a scene. If colors are not assigned properly, the ability to perceive depth in the 3D scene will be negatively affected.

C909.name: Continuous intensity value
C909.definition: Continuous intensity value is a real number, typically normalized, that lighting models use to compute colors. These values usually fall within the range of 0 to 1.

C910.name: Reflection coefficient or reflectivity
C910.definition: Reflection coefficient or reflectivity is a surface property that determines the fraction of incident light that gets reflected and comes to the viewer's eye. This coefficient varies between 0.0 and 1.0, where 0 represents a dull surface and 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface.

C911.name: Diffuse light component
C911.definition: Diffuse light component is the light that is reflected in a diffuse manner when coming directly from the light source. This component accounts for the general, non-shiny reflection of light.

C912.name: Specular reflection component
C912.definition: Specular reflection component is the light that is reflected with a specular effect, which appears as a shiny bright spot. This component is calculated using an approximate model, such as the Phong model.

C913.name: Reflection coefficients
C913.definition: Reflection coefficients are three-element vectors (k, kd, ks) that must be specified for surfaces when computing color. These vectors individually specify the reflection properties for the red, green, and blue primary colors.

C914.name: Intensity attenuation over distance
C914.definition: Intensity attenuation over distance is the phenomenon where the intensity of light diminishes as the distance between the light source and the surface point increases. This factor must be accounted for in realistic rendering.

C915.name: Radial intensity attenuation
C915.definition: Radial intensity attenuation is a factor that accounts for the effect of diminishing light intensity based on the distance from the light source. This factor is typically computed using an inverse quadratic function.

C916.name: Inverse quadratic function
C916.definition: Inverse quadratic function is a mathematical expression used to compute the attenuation factor for radial attenuation. This function uses the distance between the source and the surface point as a primary variable.

C917.name: Angular intensity attenuation
C917.definition: Angular intensity attenuation is a factor used to control light visibility and brightness within a specific region. This factor is primarily considered when generating focused effects like spotlights.

C918.name: Spotlight effect
C918.definition: Spotlight effect is a visual outcome where only elements within a defined region are visible or brightly visible. Areas outside this specific zone are rendered darker.

C919.name: Colored light model
C919.definition: Colored light model is a method for assigning colors where emitted light intensity is broken down into three components corresponding to the primary colors. These three intensities combine together to give the perception of any color.

C920.name: Source intensity
C920.definition: Source intensity is a three-element vector (Is) that represents the light emitted by a colored light source. This vector consists of three components corresponding to the primary colors: red (Isr), green (Isg), and blue (Isb).

C921.name: Intensity mapping
C921.definition: Intensity mapping is the process of converting a continuous, infinite range of computed intensity values into a finite set of values supported by a display device. This process involves finding the nearest device-supported intensity value for any computed pixel intensity.

C922.name: Transformation matrix
C922.definition: Transformation matrix is a mathematical matrix used to transform a point from its local coordinate system into the world coordinate system. This matrix can be either an individual basic matrix or a composite matrix.

C923.name: Composite matrix
C923.definition: Composite matrix is a type of transformation matrix that is commonly used in rendering pipelines. It is formed by combining multiple basic matrices.

C924.name: Object representation
C924.definition: Object representation is the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline, which takes place within the local coordinate reference frame. This stage defines the object itself.

C925.name: Viewing pipeline
C925.definition: Viewing pipeline is a set of stages used in computer graphics to simulate the process of rendering a three-dimensional scene onto a two-dimensional display.

C926.name: Projection
C926.definition: Projection is the process of selecting a portion of a constructed three-dimensional scene and mapping it onto a two-dimensional display plane or view plane.

C927.name: Projection transformation
C927.definition: Projection transformation is a pipeline operation that transforms a 3D view coordinate scene into a 2D view plane description. This process maps the three-dimensional geometry onto a two-dimensional surface.

C928.name: Window-to-viewport transformation
C928.definition: Window-to-viewport transformation transforms the projected scene from a 2D view plane description into a 2D device coordinate space. This final transformation prepares the scene for display on the device.

C929.name: Clipping
C929.definition: Clipping is an operation that takes place within the 3D view coordinate system. It is one of the two operations that occur during the viewing pipeline.

C930.name: Hidden surface removal
C930.definition: Hidden surface removal is an operation that takes place within the 3D view coordinate system. This process determines which surfaces are visible and which are obscured by other objects in the scene.

C931.name: View coordinate system
C931.definition: View coordinate system is a coordinate system that has its own axes (u, n, and v) and is used to represent the scene from the camera's perspective. This system is established based on the parameters of the camera.

C932.name: Camera parameters
C932.definition: Camera parameters are the specific values used to define the view coordinate system. These parameters include the camera position, the view of point, the view direction, and the center of interest or look-at point.

C933.name: Orthogonal axes
C933.definition: Orthogonal axes are three mutually perpendicular axes (N, V, and U) that are determined using camera parameters. These three axes together define the view coordinate system.

C934.name: View plane
C934.definition: View plane is the two-dimensional surface onto which three-dimensional objects in the view coordinate system are projected. This surface transforms the world coordinate description into a 2D view plane description.

C935.name: Clipping window
C935.definition: Clipping window is a rectangular area that is often used to define the boundaries of the view plane. Different terminologies may be used to refer to this concept.

C936.name: View volume
C936.definition: View volume is a three-dimensional region within the scene that determines which portion of the scene will be projected onto the view plane. This volume defines the specific area of the scene that the system is intended to project.

C937.name: Perspective projection
C937.definition: Perspective projection is a type of projection that requires converting the frustum into a parallel canonical view volume, which is a normalized unit cube. This conversion involves both scaling and shearing operations.

C938.name: Parallel projection
C938.definition: Parallel projection is a type of projection where the canonical view volume can be obtained by simply scaling the arbitrarily defined view volume. This method is computationally simpler than perspective projection.

C939.name: Canonical view volume
C939.definition: Canonical view volume is a concept used to simplify pipeline computations in rendering. It involves converting any defined view volume, regardless of its shape or size, into a normalized cube.

C940.name: Normalized cube
C940.definition: Normalized cube is a standard cube used to define the view volume. It is the result of converting any arbitrary view volume into a standardized shape and size.

C941.name: Window
C941.definition: Window is a normalized clipping window, which is also typically referred to as the view plane. This representation is an abstract intermediate representation and has no direct relation to the display.

C942.name: Viewport
C942.definition: Viewport is a portion of the final screen defined in device space where the scene will be rendered. It is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and dimensions.

C943.name: Homogeneous coordinate representation
C943.definition: Homogeneous coordinate representation is a coordinate system used in the transformation process. To return to a Cartesian point, the obtained point must be divided by the homogeneous factor W.

C944.name: VR resource optimization
C944.definition: VR resource optimization refers to resource optimization concerns that are typically encountered when dealing with immersive experiences. This focus is specific to the challenges presented by immersive experiences.

C945.name: Rendering process
C945.definition: Rendering process is the field of computer graphics that deals with the most challenging part of generating an immersive experience. This process is central to the creation of immersive experiences.

C946.name: Projection transformation
C946.definition: Projection transformation is the process of transforming coordinates from the 3D view coordinate system to the 2D view coordinate system. This transformation is a key step in the graphics pipeline.

C947.name: Device coordinate system
C947.definition: Device coordinate system is a continuous coordinate system where the coordinate values can be any real number. This system describes the space on a display device before the image is rendered.

C948.name: Pixel grid
C948.definition: Pixel grid is a structure of a display device that uses discrete coordinates. Points on this grid must have integer coordinates because they represent individual pixels.

C949.name: Discrete coordinate system
C949.definition: Discrete coordinate system is a coordinate system where coordinates can only be integer values. This type of system is required when representing points on a pixel grid.

C950.name: Line rendering
C950.definition: Line rendering is a common activity within computer graphics that involves drawing lines onto an image. It serves as the fundamental basis for any image rendering process.

C951.name: Bresenham's line drawing algorithm
C951.definition: Bresenham's line drawing algorithm is a popular and well-known algorithm used to find the pixels that approximate a line. It achieves this by performing computations using only integer arithmetic to avoid slowing down the computer.

C952.name: Floating point operations
C952.definition: Floating point operations are calculations that, when used in rendering, can significantly slow down a computer. The objective of efficient algorithms is to avoid these operations when rendering lines.

C953.name: Anti-aliasing operations
C953.definition: Anti-aliasing operations are additional processes used to remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing. These operations ensure a better visual effect for the rendered image.

C954.name: Graphics library
C954.definition: A graphics library is an existing implementation that programmers can import into their programming environment. These libraries provide APIs to handle graphics-related concerns and deal with the lower-level tasks involved in computer graphics.

C955.name: Layered architecture
C955.definition: Layered architecture is a structural form used to understand the overall virtual reality system, where components are stacked sequentially from top to bottom.

C956.name: VR application layer
C956.definition: VR application layer is the highest layer in the architecture where the actual virtual reality application resides.

C957.name: VR engine
C957.definition: VR engine is the component responsible for allowing developers to handle graphics using provided APIs without needing direct access to native rendering libraries.

C958.name: Native rendering library
C958.definition: Native rendering library is a library that the VR engine calls upon to execute rendering activities, such as OpenGL or Vulkan.

C959.name: Parallelism
C959.definition: Parallelism is the characteristic of graphics operations where multiple tasks can be performed simultaneously. This ability to process data at the same time allows for a significant gain in performance, which is crucial for real-time rendering.

C960.name: Multicore system
C960.definition: A multicore system is a type of hardware that contains a large number of cores or unit processing elements. These cores work together to perform operations simultaneously.

C961.name: Streaming multiprocessor unit
C961.definition: A streaming multiprocessor unit is a grouping of cores within a GPU. These cores are capable of performing simple integer and floating-point arithmetic operations.

C962.name: Rasterization stage
C962.definition: Rasterization stage determines which pixels on the screen overlap with the device space triangles. This stage exploits inherent parallelism by treating each pixel independently.

C963.name: Surface texturing
C963.definition: Surface texturing is a pixel processing activity where the computed color is replaced by the color of a stored texture image. This method applies texture images to the geometry being rendered.

C964.name: Depth buffer
C964.definition: Depth buffer is a dedicated memory used by GPUs for hidden surface removal. It stores the distance of the viewer from each pixel in a 3D scene before projection onto a 2D plane.
